Well, I can speak as regards the "final and the binding," but I am not sure that I can speak as regards the "other", until I know what the "other" is. Nothing can be done of a final and binding nature-nothing whatever. This stands to reason, because this is a conference-this is not an executive. Even the War Cabinet was not an executive; it was a consultative body and nothing more. In that relation I would suggest that hon. members opposite, anyway, read the comments of the late Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier on the objects and nature of the War Cabinet and on the desirability of some such body meeting periodically, even from year to year. It was a consultative body, this is a consultative body-a body whereby the various units that compose the Empire can meet, get each other's opinions, learn each other's conditions, then come back to the parliaments from which they are sent and, in the light of the information there gained, in the light of the impressions there driven home upon them, in the light of knowledge as to conditions, not only in' their own country but in the world at large, make such recommendations to their home parliaments as to them seem best suited to meet the need. That will be the nature of this conference, and in that respect it is on a parity with conferences held before, whether Imperial conferences or war cabinets. I can give the assurance, with all the emphasis that I can command, that no step whatever will be taken binding this country-indeed, no step can be taken, whatever might be the will of the representative of Canada, which would have force or effect before ratification by the Parliament of this Dominion.

My right
hon. friend has omitted to make any reference to the correspondence. I asked him if he would state whether the House would be furnished with copies of any correspondence which had taken place.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Well, in answer to
that I can say this: The question of the bringing down of correspondence leading to conclusions is a question the proper disposition of which I think every parliament in the world understands; I know this parliament does. No one will understand
t

it better than my hon. friend from Maison-neuve (Mr. Lemieux). He will recall that when he was instrumental in arriving at certain conclusions with Japan he and his government distinctly refused to bring down correspondence covering the negotiations leading thereto. What is the reason for the adoption of this principle? It is because if negotiations, proposals, counterproposals leading to conclusions, are to be divulged, then in a succeeding case there will be no proposals or counter-proposals because the countries will not make them. It is essential if there is to be success that the seal of secrecy shall be maintained. It is sometimes possible that certain papers can be brought down with the consent of all concerned. So far as I am concerned, at the moment I cannot recall anything signed by this country or signed by any representative of this country which, if the other correspondence could be brought down, could not be brought down as well. But these are marked by the senders as secret and confidential and are held as such-usually permanently held as such; sometimes held as such subject afterwards by consent to be disclosed.

Mr. Speaker, I intend to address the House only for a few moments. As has been said by the right hon. member for King's (Sir Robert Borden) this question is above party politics and it should be approached from the broadest point of view. I therefore speak this afternoon not as a party man but as a Canadian, as a British subject in Canada, on this all-absorbing question of our relations with the Mother Country, in view of the coming Conference of Prime Ministers to be held in the month of June.
I cannot understand how the Prime Minister can object to the motion offered by my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King). It is couched in very moderate language and should be accepted by the Government as a friendly advice in connection with the conference which the right hon. the Prime Minister will attend as Canada's representative. The question of our relations, Mr. Speaker, with the Mother Country and with the other parts of the Empire is perhaps the most important question from a national standpoint affecting as it does the powers of the Canadian Parliament and, above all, the rights of the Canadian people. The Prime Minister should be grateful to this Parliament if it chooses to back up the attitude he will take at the conference by 
setting forth its considered opinion with respect to certain vital matters.
I listened with great pleasure to the chapter of constitutional history given to the House this afternoon by the right hon. member for King's. In my judgment the right hon. gentleman has practically graduated to the coming ministry of foreign affairs for Canada. His remarks were certainly very interesting, and I am pleased to note that since he has been out of office he has been most generous toward his late great opponent,-I have reference to his immediate predecessor. He has been generous enough to associate the name of Laurier with the makers of Canada, with those statesmen who since 1841, were so intimately connected with our constitutional development. Let me reciprocate the thought and say at once that he himself has made some history during the last few years and that in his capacity as the representative of Canada he has done us great service. But let us be frank about these Imperial conference or Imperial cabinet meetings. Let us be candid about all such gatherings in London: they, are in a sense much more sentimental and academic than practical. But, they would be dangerous if we did not, as we intend to do to-day, clearly define the attitude which should be taken by Qur representatives and map out the scope of their mandate. Speaking for myself, and, I am sure, for the majority in this House, I am proud that Canada in June next shall be represented by the right hon. gentleman who now occupies the position of Prime Minister of this Dominion (Mr. Meighen). It is fitting and proper that such conferences should be held from time to time in order to demonstrate to the whole world the moral power of the British Empire. We may be asked at the outset: What is the status of Canada? I may answer at once that pur status has not been altered by recent events. As I have had occasion to say before, it matters not what has been the' effort of Canada during the last great war, it matters not what part Canada might have taken at previous Imperial War Cabinet meetings, there is but one country in the Empire which fully possesses her Sovereignty, and that is the United Kingdom. Canada is indeed a great Dominion, vested with the fullest powers of self-government, but she is not sovereign. As the right hon. gentleman stated a moment ago, self-government has been acquired gradually from year to year, from decade to decade: First of all, Canada was a Crown

colony, and as such her public works, for instance, were under the direction of engineers of the home Government. The Rideau canal, in Ottawa, the Lachine canal near Montreal and all the public works which were started under the Union, were built under the direction of engineers sent out by the home Government. Our post office for many years was managed from London, and our own tariff was prepared by the Chancellor of the Exchequer. The right hon. gentleman a moment ago, as he was mentioning the names of Lafontaine, Baldwin, Macdonald, Cartier, Blake and Laurier, cited also the name of Sir Alexander T. Galt. If Canada is sepecially indebted to any man for having many and many years ago asserted the rights of this country to her fullest fiscal autonomy, that gratitude is due to the late Sir Alexander T. Galt, a son of old Scotland, who settled in the Eastern Townships and who was for many years the trusted representative of the English-speaking minority in my province. It is well, now that his life has been recently published, that I should quote the words of Sir Alexander T. Galt, when he was claiming from the home Government that right which we have now of making our own tariff and even of taxing British goods. He said:
Self-government would be utterly annihilated if the views of the Imperial Government were to he preferred to those of the people of Canada. It is, therefore, the duty of the present Government distinctly to affirm the right of the Canadian legislature to adjust the taxation of the people in the way they deem best-even if it should unfortunately happen to meet the disapproval of the Imperial ministry. Her Majesty cannot he advised to disallow such acts, unless her advisers are prepared to assume the administration of the affairs of the Colony, irrespective of the views of its inhabitants.
The Imperial Government are not responsible for the debts and engagements of Canada, they do not maintain its judicial, educational, or civil service, they contribute nothing to the internal government of the country, and the provincial Legislature, acting through a ministry directly responsible to it, has to make provision respecting all these wants ; they must necessarily claim and exercise the widest latitude as to the nature and extent of the burthens to be placed upon the industry of the people. The provincial Government believes that His Grace must share their own convictions on this important subjeot, but as serious evil would have resulted had His Grace taken a different course, it is wiser to prevent future complication by distinctly stating the position that must be maintained by every Canadian administration.
Sir, we do not enjoy Sovereignty; but as I stated a moment ago, we have the fullest powers of self-government, as boldly asserted in the fifties by the late
finance minister of the Canadian Government, Sir Alexander T. Galt. His principles apply to-day with equal force as they did in those days in regard to the tariff question. The right hon. gentleman, when attending the conference, can very well repeat after Sir A. T. Galt: " selfgovernment would be utterly annihiliated if the views of the Imperial Government were to be preferred to those of the people of Canada." The leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) is only expressing, in a few concrete words, the broad principle ' asserted by Sir Alexander T. Galt sixty years ago, by stating:
That the House, while recognizing the propriety of Canada being represented at any Imperial Conference or conference of the Prime Ministers of the Umpire that may be called, desires to record its opinion that at the coming conference no step should be taken in any way involving any change ip the relations of Canada to other parts of the Empire ; and that, in view of the present financial position of Canada, no action should he takem implying any obligations on the part of Canada to undertake new expenditures for naval or military purposes.
No conference of Dominion Prime Ministers, no Imperial statesmen can object to a direction given to the right hon. gentleman by the representatives of the Canadian people in Parliament assembled. The powers which we constitutionally possess cannot be abridged by any conference, by any imperial cabinet outside of this Parliament which the proper forum and the expressive power, limited though it may be, by the British North America Act.
My right hon. friend, who applauded a moment ago the name of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and who will, I am confident he inspired by his policy in this Imperial Conference, might well adopt the words which were uttered by the great Canadian statesman at the last conference which he attended in 1911, and which brought to him encomiums of the Prime Minister of Great Britain, Mr. Asquith, when he said of Sir Wilfrid that he indeed was the Nestor of that conference. You will remember that Sir Wilfrid Laurier proclaimed on that occasion that Imperial unity, in which he believed, should be based on full local autonomy. The principle of autonomy in Canada, as in Australia, South Africa, Newfoundland and New Zealand, is the keystone of the whole Imperial structure.
The right hon. gentleman a moment ago enumerated academic questions which, as I stated, can well be brought up, without any special direction to be received from this Parliament, at the next Imperial Conference; for instance, such questions as

that of cable and postal rates, of wireless, of copyright, of an Imperial Statistical Bureau, of the renewal of the Japanese Treaty. I wish to state at once in answer to what my right hon. friend suggested a moment ago, that certain correspondence must be regarded as strictly confidential. I quite agree with him that correspondence respecting the relation of one country to another, that is to say, affecting two foreign countries, must be regarded as strictly confidential. At the Foreign Office in Great Britain they would not allow even a minister of one of the Dominions to have access to some of the documents which are on the shelves there. But as regards correspondence that affect only the relations between the Mother Country and Canada, for instance, while a portion of them may be considered confidential, others can . properly be laid on the Table. I am surprised that we have not had laid on the Table of the House the correspondence between the Canadian Government and the Home Government as regards the preparation for the coming Conference in the month of June; as to who took the initiative, what were the suggestions made, without, of course, involving any matter of foreign policy; who is so particularly insistent that the right hon. gentleman shall leave Canada at the present time, when the financial situation is so involved here, and go to the other side to discuss Imperial problems? I say that the right hon. gentleman might well have laid that correspondence on the Table. However, I shall not dispute with him over the absence of the papers.
At the coming Conference, personally I do not object to the discussion of trade matters, although Canada is acting towards the Mother Country in her own way as regards the framing of tariffs. Long ago Canada cut her moorings with the Home Government on fiscal matters. We tax the goods of the Mother Country as we see fit. True it is that Canada, a few years ago, on the initiative of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) gave the Mother Country a Preference. I do not object to that question being debated at the coming Conference; perhaps the preference might be extended to some of the other dominions, always bearing in mind, of course, that in all these matters of trade, Canada is absolutely free to act as she pleases. For my part, I would not object to increasing the British preference. My right hon. friend, however, must not forget that he will meet at that Conference,
[Mr. Lemieux.l .
at the head of the table, the present Colonial Secretary, the Right Hon. Mr. Winston Churchill, who has established a tradition for himself on the question of the British preference. It will be remembered, Mr. Speaker, that when a trade preference was granted to Great Britain by Canada, a statesman in Canada and another in Great Britain at once took up the cudgels in favour of a reciprocal preference. Mr. Chamberlain was the apostle of that idea in Great Britain, and I think my right hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce was its eloquent advocate, not only in Canada, but even in Great Britain. He will remember the answer given by the Right Hon. Mr. Winston Churchill, who will preside at the conference when it meets in London in June next.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I do not want my
words to affect anybody, but the gentleman who will preside at the conference will be the Prime Minister of Great Britain. He presided at the Imperial Cabinet. In his absence, the Prime Minister of the senior Dominion presided.

I accept my right hon. friend's correction. Certainly, however, the Right Hon. Winston Churchill will be present. In fact, I understand that the Conference has bieen summoned at his special request, and already, The Thunderer, the London Times, is cautioning the public against the enterprising nature of Mr. Winston Churchill. Mr. Churchill took a very drastic attitude on the reciprocal preference some ten years ago. He proclaimed that if the dominions were going to exact from the Mother Country a reciprocal preference, he, having regard to British interests exclusively, would bang, bar, and bolt the door. So my right hon. friend should not be afraid of getting moderate instructions from the Canadian Parliament before he meets a gentleman who has used such-shall I say?-violent language in reply to the agitation started in Canada by my right hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and in England by the late Mr. Joseph Chamberlain.
I now come to the question of defence. Indeed, do not all these questions revolve around our share of Imperial defence both on land and sea? Why all these shams? Let us meet boldly the issue which presents itself as between the Dominions and the Mother Country. The whole object of these Conferences, and of these frantic appeals made by certain people in the

Mother Land to the Dominions, is to draft a binding agreement on the question of Imperial defence on land and sea. Read Mr. Curtis' book; read the speeches of that most eminent of Imperalists, the late Mr. Joseph Chamberlain; follow closely his last great campaign after the Boer War; scan the reports of the various conferences at which he presided when the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier and other Dominion statesmen were convened in London and you will at once realize that the paramount question at issue is that of defence. Mr. Chamberlain put it in a very blunt way. In his mind the i only question, Mr. Speaker, was whether or not the weary Titan, old John Bull, should carry the load alone, or should the Dominions share the burden of expenditure? That is the issue. Why should we evade it? Why should we not face it, discuss it, without equivocation and take a firm stand upon it, either for or against? Do you not think, Mr. Speaker, that on such an issue, which involves not only a tremendous expenditure, but indeed the very future of Canada, the hands of the right hon. gentleman should be strengthened by an expression of opinion of the Canadian Parliament? Should he not be instructed that he must not bind the future of this country at that Conference unless the Canadian Parliament has passed final judgment on any issue?
Mr. Speaker, let me say to the school which is perhaps less represented in the House of Commons than it is in the various organizations throughout the land, in the round clubs for instance, that Canada has done nobly her part in the last great war. She has every right in. the world to be proud of the splendid share she took in that world conflict. There was no necessity for any binding agreement with the Mother Country in 1914. Parliament, immediately after it was summoned, decided that Canada should give to the Mother Country, not only her moral support, but the best that was in her. She gave her sons, 500,000 of them, and 60,000 of her bravest now sleep their last sleep in Flanders' Fields. Many thousand of the boys are now with us crippled, wounded for life. We are engaged in the process of civil re-establishment and we are morally obliged to support not only the widows and orphans of our dead, but also the. unfortunate men who have returned incapacitated. Mr. Speaker, Canada has done her share, and if there is a timorous minority in this country, or in Great Britain which is anxious to embalm in black and white some agreement by
which Canada should take part in the wars of the Empire, let that minority read the history of the last six years, and it will find in that history an adequate answer. After the war, Canada took part in the Peace Congress; she subscribed to the Versailles Treaty. Canada, as a result, is now represented and has a voice in the League of Nations. What is the object of the League of Nations? Is it to increase armaments, or to promote war? The very contrary. The object of the league is to put an end to all wars, and to settle by way of arbitration all disputes arising between nations. It is intended to usher a new era, the era of disarmament, which in the past the great powers of Europe should have endeavoured to bring about. Therefore Canada should shun all offers that are made to embark her in a new race towards armaments. In that connection I am somewhat at a loss to understand my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen). He seems to believe that no final decision will be arrived at by that conference. Of course, I accept his word. But, on the other hand, the cables from the other side every morning and evening remind us that this conference will be the most important in the history of the relations of the Mother Country with her Dominions. Mr. Lloyd George, the British Prime Minister, is reported on the 15th of last month as follows:	[DOT]
The defence of the Empire was a great problem, which ought to be an Imperial concern. It was too much to ask small islands to undertake the defence of this gigantic Empire in every sea. At the forthcoming conference of the Prime Ministers of the Empire, the whole problem of Imperial defence would be considered. There must be co-ordination, not between the various services only, but between the several parts of the Empire.
Sir, this is a concrete proposal, it is a large order; it is a definite programme, and we have a right, it seems to me, to caution the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen), in the discussions that will arise. He may tell his colleagues at that conference that he may hearken to them, he may even offer advice. But, Sir, not until that advice has been backed up by public opinion in Canada, and has been ratified by the Canadian Parliament, can it be anything but advice and tentative suggestion. Mr. Speaker, my right hon. friend, I am sure, will not forget to inform the Home authorities and the members of the conference of the present financial situation of Canada. Our national
You forget 1837.
1837, the Rebellion. That was before we got responsible government under Lord Elgin during the Baldwin-Lafontaine administration. It was in a "seven" year anyway.
Yes, a lucky number.

1867, Confederation;
1887, the first Colonial Conference-the first occasion on which the representatives of the Dominions were called together for consultation with the representatives of the Motherland on matters of common concern to the whole Empire; 1907, provision for a permanent Imperial Conference meeting every four years, with a fixed secretariat and a definite class of subjects for consideration; 1907, the first meeting of the Imperial War Cabinet and the passage of the resolution, to which reference has already been made, providing for the calling of this constitutional conference.
As the resolution referred to by the Prime Minister this afternoon is the authority under which this constitutional conference is to be called, I shall read it to the House. It was passed at the Imperial War Conference in 1917, and is in these terms:
The Imperial War Conference are of opinion that the readjustment of the constitutional relations of the component parts of the Empire is too important and intricate a subject to he dealt with during the war, and that it should form the subject of a special Imperial Conference to be summoned as soon as possible after the cessation of hostilities. They deem it their duty, however, to place on record their view that any such readjustment, while thoroughly preserving all existing powers of self-government, and complete control of domestic affairs, should be based upon a full recognition of the Dominions as autonomous nations of an Imperial Commonwealth, and of India as an important portion of the same, should recognize the right of the Dominions and India to an adequate voice in foreign policy and in foreign relations, and should provide effective arrangements for continuous consultation in all important matters of common Imperial concern, and for such necessary concerted action, founded on consultation, as the several governments may determine.
It is the conference authorized by this resolution which is referred to in the agenda submitted by the Prime Minister to the House, and the conference of Prime Ministers will give preliminary consideration to the question of the calling of this conference. It is not without importance for us to recall that this resolution was submitted to Parliament by the then Prime Minister in 1917 on his return from the Imperial Conference of that year, and the resolution was then discussed, members on both sides of the House taking part, including the late distinguished leader of the Opposition, the right hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier. So this resolution, indicating the lines along which our constitutional development is to proceed, has been before the people of Canada for the past four years, people of Canada for the past four years,

and so far as I am aware no objection has been made to the principles expressed in the resolution.
The right hon. member for King's this afternoon referred to the importance of the Conference of 1907 which established the Imperial Conference on a permanent basis. I just wish to read a brief extract from an article published in the Round Table magazine shortly after the holding of that conference, which indicates the importance and significance of the great step taken in the year 1907:
This resolution established the status of the Dominions as national entities, entirely distinct from that which inhabited the British Isles. It recognized that the basis of Imperial organization was the co-operation of five nations, not the centralization of power in the hands of the British Government as an Imperial Parliament. It finally destroyed the older conception of Imperial development, as a gradual reunion of the colonies with the Mother Country through representatives in either of the British Houses of Parliament.
I submit that is a very clear and admirable statement of the effect of the resolution of the Imperial Conference of 1907.
I do not intend this evening to enter into a discussion of the question of Canada's status. I only wish to follow this particular resolution -by a statement published in the report of the Imperial War Cabinet in the year 1918. This statement is of importance to us because it is not our statement, but that of the Imperial Government itself in the official publication of the proceedings of the War Cabinet. It reads as follows:
The common effort and sacrifice In the war have inevitably led to the recognition of an equality of status between the responsible governments of the Empire. This equality has long been acknowledged in principle and found its adequate expression in 1917 in the creation or, rather-, natural coming into being of an Imperial War Cabinet as an instrument for evolving a common Imperial policy in the conduct of the war. The nature of the constitutional development involved in the establishment as a permanent institution of the Imperial Cabinet system was clearly explainedi by Sir Robert Borden in a speech to the Empire Parliamentary Association on June 21, 19'18.
The report then quotes with approval an extract from an address made by the former Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden), before the British Empire Parliamentary Association-a statement which is in accordance with that made by him to the House to-day as well as other statements made by him to this House on former occasions-with reference to our present constitutional position. The result of this development, Mr. Speaker, cannot be bet-

ter illustrated than in the contrast presented between the conditions in 1911 and in 1921. In 1911 the Prime Minister of Canada and the prime ministers of the other Dominions were admitted to a meeting of the Committee of Imperial Defence, where for the first time in the history of the Dominions, a British foreign secretary reviewed before the prime ministers of the Dominions, the various aspects of British foreign policy; they were initiated, as Mr. Asquith pointed out, into the very heart of the secrets of the foreign policy of the British Empire. That was an entirely new departure-as Mr. Asquith said a departure of great constitutional significance. But when we compare that position in 1911-the Prime Minister invited in as a favour, so to speak, to sit with the Committee of Imperial Defence and to hear a review of foreign policy-with the position in 1921-the Parliament of Canada exercising its proper and legitimate functions of discussing questions of foreign policy affecting the whole Empire -we have the best possible evidence of the development in our status during the past ten years. When the Prime Minister of Canada meets with the Prime Minister of Great Britain and the prime ministers of the other Dominions in London he does so, not as the representative of a subordinate power in the presence of a representative of a 'superior power, but on an absolute equality with the Prime Minister of Great . Britain and the prime ministers of the other Dominions of the Empire.
Some question has been raised as to why this conference should be held and why a constitutional conference is necessary. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that such a conference is necessary, not to frame any new written constitution-I think it would be a misfortune if any constitutional conference undertook to frame a written constitution for the British Empire. The strength of our constitution may be what some would consider as its weakness. The strength of our constitution is that it is not written, therefore it has all the flexibility necessary to meet changing conditions as they arise from time to time in the different stages of the development of the Empire. But such a conference is necessary to put at rest all this discussion about the status of the Dominions. Why should we be discussing in this Parliament, why should they be discussing in the Australian Parliament, why should they be discussing in the Parliaments of New Zealand and South Africa, the question of the status of
the Dominions? The Constitutional Conference should not create for us any new status, but by a declaration in which all the governments of the Empire join, they should recognize our present constitutional position and the constitutional position of all the Dominions as being equal in status with the Mother Country as self-governing nations of the British Empire.
Another reason why we should hold that constitutional conference is that coupled with such a declaration of status-and, in my humble judgment, made at the same time-should be an outline of plans for consultation and co-operation between the Mother Country and the Dominions in matters of common concern to the whole Empire. Plans which while fully preserving the freedom and self-government of the Dominions, would ensure the strength and security.of the whole. For I feel quite sure that'members of this House stand for two principles, first, for the full equality of status of the Dominions with the Mother Country as self-governing nations of the British Empire, and second, for preserving the strength and unity of the Empire as a whole.
What should be the procedure at the conference? May I venture to offer one or two suggestions? First, as to the programme. I doubt if the programme should cover any more than the working out of the two problems I have mentioned, one the declaration respecting the existing status, and the other, plans and methods of co-operation in connection with foreign affairs of common concern to the whole Empire.
The question of representation is not without difficulty. I am inclined to share the view expressed by the hon. member for King's when he discussed this matter in the House on a former occasion, namely, that it would be desirable in this constitutional conference not only that the Government should be represented but that the Opposition of the day, the different interests represented in the House of Commons, should have representation in the conference. That, of course, could not be done by one country unless done by all countries, but my reason for supporting that view is the one given by the hon. member for King's last year, that in matters affecting our constitutional relations we should proceed as a united people rather than divided on party lines. As regards the date and place of meeting of the constitutional conference, I have no suggestion to make, except to express an

earnest hope that the conference will be held in the Dominion of Canada. I think it will be a real advantage, not only to the Mother Country, but to Canada and all the other portions of the Empire, if this conference affecting the future relations of the Empire is held in one of the Domijiions, and Canada, as the senior and the largest Dominion, would have the first claim to that conference.
The next matter on which I wish to make a few observations is in reference to military, naval and air defence. The one aspect of the matter, which apparently, to judge from statements that have been made in Great Britain, is likey to assume the greatest importance if the subject comes up for serious consideration, is that of naval defence. In that respect, I wish to express my entire concurrence with the view presented by the right hon. member for King's (Sir Robert Borden) and with the view presented by the Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) this afternoon, that the time is not opportune to take up and deal with that important problem. I desire to give very briefly my reasons for that conclusion. Lest any hon. member should misunderstand my position on the general question of naval defence, I have no hesitation in stating it to the House, and I do not desire to depart, by even the change of a word, from the statement of policy which I made at the Montreal Reform Club on November 11, 1911.
Good old days. '

I do not change my
principles. This is what I said:
In the matter of naval defence the time for talking is past, the time for action has come. We should he ashamed to permit the people of Great Britain-financially burdened as they are and must continue to be in working out great measures of social reform for the benefit of the masses of the people-to not only bear their own burden of naval defence, but to bear ours as well. Our action should be adequate, commensurate with our ability and our share of the burden. Our policy should not be the product of a momentary enthusiasm or of unworthy fear, but as part of a permanent and well-considered plan whereby Canada will undertake her share in the defence of the Empire. Let our policy not be formed by or shaped in response to the spirit of militarism. Our navy is not for aggression, but for the defence of our coasts, and the protection of our trade routes : for the maintenance of the traditions and ideals for which our British system of Government and our flag stand.
If conditions to-day were the same as they were in 1912, that is exactly where I would stand to-day. But I agree with the view presented by the right hon. member

for King's and the Prime Minister, that as a result of the great war a radical change has taken place in the situation. The cause of apprehension at that time was the existence of the German navy. That navy has ceased to be. Under the provisions of the Treaty of Peace, not only has the German navy ceased to be, but Germany cannot build a new navy. Her right to build is absolutely limited and defined by the terms of the treaty. Any menace that existed from Germany and the German navy has been removed as a result of the war. Not only has that been removed, but in the terms of the treaty itself, provision has been made for the limitation of armaments. I want to draw attention to a provision that I rather fear that some of the signatories to the treaty sometimes forget. Part V, military, naval and air clauses, states:
In order to render possible the initiation of a general limitation of the armaments of all nations, Germany undertakes strictly to observe the military, naval and air clauses which follow.
In other words, the signatories to the Treaty, in laying the foundation for the clauses strictly limiting the strength of the German military, naval and air forces and in imposing similar limitations on all the other former enemy States, gave as a basic reason the possibility of initiating a general movement for the world-wide limitation of armaments. The matter, however, does not rest there. When they framed the Covenant of the League of Nations, they incorporated a special article dealing with this very matter. Article 8 of the covenant provides:
The members of the League recognise that the maintenance of peace requires the reduction of national armaments to the lowest point consistent with national safety and the enforcement by common action of international obligations.
The Council, taking account of the geographical situation and circumstances of each State, shall formulate plans for such reduction for the consideration and action of the several Governments.
' Then the Financial Conference meeting in Brussels in August last and studying the financial conditions, particularly of the countries of Europe, a conference representing all nations members of the league, placed on record their solemn conviction that the rehabilitation of the finances of Europe, and the restoration of the economic conditions of the world, could not be brought about unless there was a substantial limitations of armaments, and a large reduction in the budgets for maintaining armed forces. Therefore, we have the terms

of the treaty; the Covenant of the League of Nations and the recommendation of the Brussels Financial Conference, all to one effect, the importance and urgency of the limitations of armaments. I submit to the Government, as we are signatories to that treaty, as we are members of thte League of Nations, it is the bounden duty of the Government to exert its influence to the utmost, to see that every honest effort is put forward to carry out the intention of the treaty, the provisions of the covenant and the recommendation of the Brussels Financial Conference, to secure a worldwide agreement for the limitation of armaments.
I may be told that everybody is in agreement with this idea, and that the only difficulty is that certain important states are outside the league at present I recognise the difficulty created by very important States being outside. I recognise there can be no general and world-wide agreement for limitation of armaments which does not include the great nation to the south. I believe they have a unique opportunity of taking the leadership in this matter. But it would he mere hypocrisy for one to stand up here and say that he believes that all the people in all the other nations are in favour of the limitation of armaments. I do not believe they are. I believe there are militarists in every nation, who do not believe in the limitation of armaments, who believe in the sword as the method of settling international disputes and who want to maintain large armies in order that they may settle their disputes in that manner and wherever the spirit of militarism exists it is a menace to the peace of the world. I stand here to urge upon the Government to put forward every effort in their power to see that states, parties to this covenant, should endeavour to reach a solution of this problem before we are called upon to consider the other question of what share we shall take in the defence of the Empire. Should all efforts fail, should it be impossible after every honest effort has been put forth to secure such an agreement, and it appears that no agreement is possible through no fault of the British Empire, or any part of the British Empire, but because other nations will not co-operate and will still maintain the right to settle disputes by the sword, I do not hesitate to say that Canada (should be prepared to protect her own coasts and her own trade, and thus undertake her legitimate share in the naval defence of the Empire. But that situation cannot arise before this conference, and therefore I believe that Canada's position at the conference should be that we are not prepared to consider any further steps towards increasing our naval or military burdens or adding to our naval or military strength until we are satisfied that these other efforts are without avail. I am in hopes that they will not be without avail. It would be a confession of the bankruptcy of modern statesmanship, it would be a confession to the failure of our Christian civilization, if after the loss and suffering and horrors of this war the statesmen of the world could not get together and agree to reduce the armaments of the world, and free men for productive employment. No question of naval policy arises. The question of policy was settled, and settled, I judge, in accordance with the view of this Government at the time of the Imperial War Conference in 1918. The Prime Minister has read to us this afternoon the conclusion reached by the Prime Ministers of the Overseas Dominions at the Imperial Conference of 1918, and I understood him to give his endorsement to that policy. That policy has not been questioned and when the time comes, if it ever should come, that we should take further steps to increase our naval forces we already have a settled policy and defined lines along which such development should proceed.
Turning from the questions relating to our inter-imperial relations to those relating to our international relations, one passes into a field of greater difficulty. What plans should be adopted to secure unity in foreign policy in matters affecting the whole Empire is a question for the Constitutional' Conference. It cannot be settled finally until that conference is held. However, as the agenda does suggest some preliminary consideration of the question, may I venture to submit to the Government, with great deference, certain lines along which, from our Canadian standpoint, Imperial policy in foreign affairs might proceed.
May I say first, Mr. Speaker, that I entirely agree with the view presented by the Prime Minister himself, that the policy should be to pursue certain general and well understood lines of action. If we are to have a policy on international affairs, affecting the Empire as a whole, it must be a policy which all the states of the Empire can understand and follow. It therefore must

pursue certain general and well understood lines.
The first question that will arise, and it arises on the very threshold of the consideration of this problem is this: Shall the foreign policy of the Empire in the future be based on the old ideas of international relationships preceding the war, or shall it be based on the new conception of international relationships subsequent to the war? Shall it be based on the old idea of the balance of power, secret alliances and treaties, or on the new conception, embodied in the League of Nations, of international co-operation with every other nation of the world that is prepared to be friendly? I respectfully submit to the Government that the Empire policy should follow the new, and should eschew the old. There is no hope for this new policy unless the British Empire gives a lead. If it does give a strong lead in support of the new policy as against the old, there is reasonable hope, I venture to think, that the new policy may ultimately prevail; perhaps not at once, for it takes time to work such a revolutionary change.
The second is that there should be a distinction drawn as clearly as circumstances will permit, between questions that are of interest alone, so to speak, to one Dominion alone or to the Uuited Kingdom alone as distinguished from questions of high policy that are of interest to the whole Empire. Let me illustrate what I mean by questions of interest to one Dominion, and one Dominion alone. Take the questions that have arisen from time to time and are arising to-day between Canada and the United States, questions which we take up indirectly in some cases, more directly in others, and which we settle ourselves with the United States, questions which I hope in the very near future we will take up directly all the time through a Canadian minister at Washington. The settled policy of the Empire to-day is that on these questions exclusively affecting Canada, our view is accepted; and the matter is not dealt with from London, it is dealt with from Ottawa, London being informed of our conclusions. Now a distinction should be drawn between questions of that class which relate exclusively to one of the Dominions or to the Mother Country, and questions of high Imperial policy affecting the whole Empire. Dealing with the latter class, because those are the questions that are to be considered when the time comes for action, may I suggest certain lines
TMr. Kowell.]
which I venture to think it would be in the interests of the whole Empire to follow. It may be said that a number of these lines of policy are already being followed. I am not going to argue whether they are or not, but I think they should form part of any recognized policy of the Empire as a whole.
First, that the Empire has no territorial ambitions or aggressive intentions. I share entirely the views expressed by the hon. member for King's (Sir Robert Borden) in reference to western Asian commitments.
Second, we should stand for the settlement of all international disputes by peaceable means. Whatever other nations may do, the British Empire as a whole should stand before the world for that great principle of international policy, viz: the settlement of all international disputes by peaceable means.
Third, to that end, and in order to aid in carrying out that policy, the British Empire should give its whole-hearted support to the League of Nations or a League of Nations-I am not now dealing with the form, but with the substance-for the preservation of the world's peace by providing a substitute for war as a means of settling international disputes. They should also give strong support to the establishment of a permanent court of international justice. I shall not discuss this question now, as it will come up for discussion on the Bill which the Minister of Justice has before the House.
Fourth, the British Empire should give leadership and genuine support to the movement for the limitation of armaments, endeavouring to secure the co-operation of the United States. I venture to think that this question is so important that, while the United States might properly take the leadership in it, if the United States does not take such leadership the British Empire should.
Fifth, we should refrain from any special or exclusive alliances with other states. We should stand in the League of Nations as the friend of every state that honourably observes its obligations and seeks to keep the peace.
I do not believe that it is humanly possible for an organization like the League of Nations to accomplish the great purposes for which it was formed, if important members of the league form offensive or defensive alliances outside the league. If one group of important states form a so-called defensive alliance, the inevitable result will be that other states will group together in similar, so-called defensive

alliances, with a consequent weakening of the moral authority and strength of the league, and a reversion to the old principle of the balance of power from which we had hoped that the war had largely freed us.
Sixth. We should endeavour to promote international co-operation in matters of common concern to the nations and thus avoid causes of international friction, promote international friendship and the general well-being of humanity.
The League of Nations already provides machinery for that international co-operation.
I now come to a matter that is of more immediate concern to Canada, and on which I hope I shall carry the judgment of the House, even though I do not carry the judgment of all outside of the House. I shall first state the principle and then give my reasons for it.
Seventh:	The recognition of Canada's
special interest in all important international questions arising between the British Empire and the United States.
Our geographical position, the volume of our trade, our hope that in the lifetime of many here, we shall be a nation, ' not of ten or fifteen millions, but of twenty-five millions of people,-all these circumstances render the question of international relations between the British Empire and the United States of supreme concern to Canada, indeed, of more vital moment to this country than to any other portion of the British Empire. I think, in view of our relations with the Mother Country and with the United States, it is just as much in the interests of the Empire as it is in the interests of Canada, that the Empire as a whole should recognize Canada's special concern in all important international questions between the British Empire and the United States.
Eighth:	I respectfully submit to the
Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen), that he would not be going beyond what is both in the interests of Canada and of the whole Empire, if he would urge as a further principle of policy though it is but a deduction from the last, that no question of real importance arising between the British Empire and the United States should be settled without consultation with Canada. We cannot render this service effictively until we have a Canadian minister resident at Washington, but when we have a minister resident there, in touch with the American Government and the British ambassador, it can be done. Even though it may be repeating what has been
said more than once I reiterate, from the knowledge that has come to me during recent years, that we do understand the British statesmen and their point of view vastly better than the people in the United States understand them, while, at the same time, we understand the American point of view very much better than the British statesmen do, and the greatest hope for permanent cordial relations and the best possible understanding between the British Empire and the United States lies in Canada's acting as an interpreter and mediator between the United States and the Empire; Canada can render a very real service to the whole Empire in that capacity.
Ninth; If the question is of purely Canadian concern, the present well settled practice is to accept the Canadian view as to its settlement. This principle should be extended, perhaps not immediately, 'but certainly eventually, to cover questions in which the clear and paramount interest is Canadian. It is going much further than we have gone before, but I believe it is a right and sound principle and one which we should recognize in the foreign policy of the Empire. It is in the light of these principles that I propose discussing the other questions to which I have referred namely, German reparations and the Anglo-Japanese Alliance.
It does not require any particular knowledge of conditions in Europe to-day for everyone earnestly to hope that a just and reasonable settlement will be secured of the most important and difficult matter of reparations. It now appears from the correspondence which has passed that the United States is likely to take part in the further negotiations, and I venture to believe that in that probability lies the hope for an early and just settlement. Mr. Speaker, my firm conviction, is that, as a result of the crimes and horrors of the war, the blood of Europe is still too hot to secure a fair, just and permanent settlement of the question, and I think it is all to the good that the United States should participate in the negotiations, because she is able to take such a view as we in Canada would take, an absolutely just view from the standpoint of Germany, and, at the same time, a view wholly sympathetic with the Allies.
In order that we may understand the present situation, it is necessary that we should recall something of the history of the reparations question. Unless a settlement is reached no one knows where this affair will end, and so I propose asking the indulgence of the House for a few minutes

while I outline the history of the matter. On October 6, 1918, the German Government, through its Chancellor, applied to the President of the United States to take steps for the restoration of peace. In the note, the following appears:
The German Government accepts as a basis for peace negotiations the programme laid down by the President of the United States in his message to Congress of January 8, 1918, and in his subsequent pronouncements, particularly in his address of September 27, 1918.
Now, I think I may safely say that the majority of the Canadian people thought that peace at that time was premature. I think the majority of the Canadian people were of the opinion that it was not in the interests of permanent peace that a settlement should be negotiated while Germany was still in occupation of territories in Prance and Belgium. That was my own view at all events; and I expressed that view at the time. May I repeat what I then said. Speaking in the city of Hamilton on October 14, 1918, I used this language :
When the German Chancellor asks us to-day: "Is it peace?" our answer should be: "What hast thou to do with peace, so long as the crimes and barbarities perpetrated by Germany in this war are neither repented of nor punished?" The future peace and security of the world demands one or the other.
Repentance means confession, restitution, reparation. When Germany confesses her crimes and makes full restitution and reparation then there may be peace. If she will not, then the war should go on until just punishment has been me meted out to her for her crimes.
' Referring to the continuance of the war, I said:
The justification, and the only justification for continuing this terrible struggle is that it involves not only the future of our Empire, but issues vitally affecting the future welfare of humanity. This war is settling questions of the sanctity of international agreements, without which there would be world-wide anarchy ; if the right of small nations .o independent existence, without which civilization would be impoverished and permanent peace would be impossible ; of the right of free democratic government to its place in the world without which human liberty would have no real value for us, or whether right or might shall be the controlling factor in international relationships; and of whether the Christian or the Pagan conception of individual and national character shall dominate the world.
We must see that these question are settled, and settled aright before we sheathe the sword which we have so reluctantly drawn. May I speak my own thoughts when I say that I do not think we should sheathe the sword until Germany, Austria and Turkey follow the example of Bulgaria, and unconditionally surrender? We have sacrificed too much already to stay our hand until the result is decisive.
Who said that?

I said that and nothing
that has come to my knowledge since leads me to conclude that I took a wrong view of the situation at that time. I believe that was the general view of the people of Canada but the fact is that the powers principally concerned, and who had the right under the conditions to decide whether those terms should be accepted or not, decided to accept them and in the note of the Allied Governments to President Wilson of November 5,1918, the following appears:
The Allied Governments have given careful consideration to the correspondence that has passed between the President of the United States and the German Government. Subject to qualifications which follow they declare their willingness to make peace with the Government of Germany on the terms of peace laid down in the President's address to Congress of January 19, 1918, and the principles of settlement enunciated in subsequent addresses.
Now what are the two qualifications? One relates to the freedom of the seas; the other relates to reparations.
Further, in the conditions of peace laid down in his address to Congress of January 8, 1918, tlhe President declared that the invaded territories must be restored.
What are the provisions of the President's address on this question? They are set forth in points VII, VIII and XI of the 14 points:
VII. Belgium, the whole world will agree, must be evacuated and restored without any attempt to limit the Sovereignty which she enjoys in common with all other free nations.
A similar provision in regard to France is found in VIII, and a similar provision in reference to Roumania, Serbia and Montenegro in XI. Referring to these provisions the Allied note continues:
The Allied Governments feel that no doubt ought to be allowed to exist as to what this provision means. By it they understand that compensation -null be made by Germany for all damage done to the civilian population of the Allies and their property by the aggressions of Germany toy land, toy sea, and from the air.
These notes formed the basis upon which the armistice was signed and upon which Germany laid down her arms. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that Germany knew the obligation she was undertaking when she made that proposal. She knew the obligation she was undertaking when she acepted it, and Germany should pay, and I believe can pay, every dollar which that obligation imposes upon her. But the matter did not rest there. When the Allied powers in Paris submitted the Peace Treaty to Germany they added to what Germany should pay under that clause, as I read it,

the obligation to provide for the pensions of all soldiers in the Allied and associated armies on the basis of the pensions of France; they also added to that the obligation, that Germany should pay all the amounts paid out by the respective governments for separation 9 p.m. allowances during the whole period of the war, on the basis of the amounts paid by France. The net result was that they imposed upon Germany an obligation beyond what they themselves believed Germany could pay, and therefore they provided that while these amounts should be fixed by the Reparations Commission that Germany should be heard as to her capacity to pay. Germany has the right to show that this amount is beyond her capacity to pay and that the total should be reduced accordingly. The uncertainty that exists to-day, the inability to fix-by a judicial tribunal, a fair arbitral commission or by the Commission on Reparations,-the exact amount of Germany's obligation, grows out of the form in which the treaty was made.
I have no information as to what Germany is able to pay, and I have no intention of expressing any opinion on the matter. But her obligation under the settlement as I have outlined it was to make compensation for damages to the civilian population and to their property. I am informed that the total amount that Germany can pay, the total amount she may be called upon to pay, will not exceed the amount necessary to fairly carry out this obligation. I do not know whether that is correct or not but I am assuming for the purpose of my argument that it is correct, and therefore there will be no injustice-to Germany in the amount she is finally called upon to pay. If that be so then what is our position and what should be our share. If the total amount paid by Germany is not more than sufficient to restore the devastated areas, and to make compensation to the civilian population, then, if Canada takes more than it is necessary to recoup us for our ships sunk at sea or other damage to civilian population, we are taking something which Great Britain or the other Allies need in order to restore their devastated areas and to compensate their civilian population. I amspeaking only for myself but I do not wish to leave this House without putting on record my conclusion on this important matter, a conclusion which is the result of careful consideration. I hope the Government of Canada will not, in the division of the amount which comes to the British
Empire, take more than that which the Minister of Justice-and I am prepared to leave it to him-will advise that Canada is entitled to receive under the terms of the settlement under which Germany laid down her arms, and if more should be allotted to us the additional amount should go to Great Britain, or the peoples that have suffered more, for the purpose of restoring the devastated areas and repaying the civilian population.
Mr. Speaker, Canada has had a noble record throughout this war. The manner in which the Dominion entered this struggle, the manner in which she aided in carrying it through to a victorious conclusion, with no selfish objects to gain and no selfish purpose to serve but solely to help to overthrow militarism, preserve the British Empire, and restore the peace of the world, has given her a position of real moral leadership on this continent. Her prompt acceptance of the Treaty of Peace and of the covenant of the League of Nations, and the manner in which she has evidenced her willingness to co-operate with all other states to provide a substitute for war as a means of settling international disputes has strengthened her claim to moral leadership. And I covet for Canada that in this matter of reparations she will take the position that she will not ask or receive a dollar more than she is clearly entitled to receive by the terms of the settlement under which Germany laid down her arms.
There is no danger of getting more.

My hon. friend says that there is no danger of getting more. This leads me to make another submission to the Government. If Canada adopts the, policy I have suggested, what is the situation that faces us if a settlement of the question of reparations is not arrived at in the pending negotiations? I do not know whether hon. members believe that the sanctions which have been imposed recently upon Germany are imposed in accordance with the terms of the Treaty of Peace or not. One would judge from press despatches that they were imposed in accordance with those terms. I have examined the treaty with great care, and I can find no express provision in the treaty under which the sanctions could be imposed. Therefore I perused with very great interest the statement of the Attorney General in the British House of Commons in this important question. He was asked, on what grounds the Govern-
2G56

ment supported the imposition of the sanctions at the time. I am going to read to the House his answer, which will be found in the British Hansard of March 18, 1921, at page 2064:
There is, first of all. Article 430, in Part 14 of the Treaty, and it provides that, in the particular cases with which it is concerned, it shall be open to the Allies to re-occupy by means of armed forces certain areas in Germany which by that time will have been first occupied and afterwards evacuated. It is quite obvious that that Article, at any rate, has no relevancy to the present proceedings.
In explanation of that I may point out that there is a group of provisions in the treaty to secure its enforcement, the most , important being the provision for the allied occupation of German territory on the south bank of the Rhine and of certain bridge heads across the river. That is authorized for a period of fifteen years, subject to certain withdrawals in case certain amounts are paid. The section to which the right hon. the Attorney General refers is the section in the treaty which permits the Allies to re-occupy this territory in case Germany should make any default after some of the troops had been withdrawn. The Attorney General proceeds:
I pass to the second which I desire specially to mention. We get a little nearer, perhaps, to what has lately been done when we come to Paragraphs 17 and 18 of the second Annex to Part 8 of the Treaty. Part 8 is the Part of the Treaty of which the subject-matter is reparation, and Paragraph 17 provides as follows:
"In case of default by Germany in the performance of any obligation under this Part of the present Treaty the Commission. ... will forthwith give notice of such default to each of the Interested Powers, and may make such recommendations as to the action to be taken in consequence of such default as it may think necessary.
The measures which the Allied and Associated Powers shall have the right to take in case of voluntary default by Germany and which Germany agrees not to regard as acts of war, may include economic and financial prohibitions and reprisals, and, in general, such other measures as the respective Governments may determine to be necessary in the circumstances."
The Attorney General comments on various clauses of the article but I have read it throughout. The Attorney General continues:
It is apparent that there have been those who have thought that it is under the express terms of that part of tlie Treaty that recent measures -or shall I call them pressure or coercion?- have been adopted and pursued. I find it difficult to accept the proposition that those orovi-sions are strictly applicable to these proceedings. May I mention one instance, which is of itself sufficient? Before the particular measures, sub-

ject to the particular conditions -which are contained in these articles, may be carried out, a certain condition precedent has to be fulfilled, that is to say, a certain notice of a certain kind', coming form a certain notice of a certain kind, coming from a certain source, has to be given. I have made inquiries, and I am told that in fact that notice was not given. The condition precedent for the application of that part of the provisions has not been performed. ' If I had to pause there and answer the question up to that point, my answer would be that the recent measures of coertion or pressure which have been taken by the Allies against Germany are not dependent upon the particular and specific remedies or sanctions set out in the Treaty.
The Attorney General* however, proceeds to give the grounds upon which those sanctions were imposed. He bases it upon the general right of victorious belligerents to enforce the performance of a treaty, and that that right is not limited by the express provisions in the Treaty; that Germany by her conduct has shown she has no intention to perform the Treaty, and that it is for the Allies, and for the Allies alone, to determine the measures necessary for its enforcement. The Minister of Justice will be able to advise on the point, but so far as I have been able to consult the authorities on international law the position would appear to be that if the proceedings are not taken pursuant to the express provisions of the Treaty under which it is agreed by Germany that certain sanctions should not be considered acts of war, military occupation outside the express terms of the Treaty is either a resumption of the old war or the beginning of a new war, though Germany may not choose to so regard it.
Now, my point is simply this. However far the Government of Canada may choose to go in co-operating for the enforcement in accordance with the express terms of the treaty to which we are parties, I submit that the Government should hesitate to take part in any programme which may involve a new war, should the Minister of Justice or the Prime Minister come to the conclusion that the imposition of these sanctions outside the treaty does amount to that. I know the view taken by very responsible parties and by certain leading journalists in England is that it does amount to a new war. The great provincial British journal, the Manchester Guardian has had a series of editorial articles on the question of the "new war," and the Observer, the strongest journalistic supporter of the present government under the very able editorship of Mr. Garvin, has had a series of articles along

somewhat similar lines. Germany should pay every dollar she agreed to pay when she laid down her arms but so far as Canada is concerned we should not go beyond the express provisions of the treaty in enforcing payment.
Just a word in conclusion in reference to the Anglo-Japanese Alliance. I have already intimated that I believe the policy of the British Empire should be that of hearty co-operation with all states rather than particular alliance with any.
The Prime Minister this afternoon referred to the terms of the Anglo-Japanese alliance. I have a copy of -the treaty in my hands and in view of its importance I propose to quote one or two paragraphs for the information of the House. The object of the treaty, as set out in clauses (a), (b) and (c) of the preamble, are as follows:
(a)	The consolidation and maintenance of the general peace in the regions of Eastern Asia and of India ;
(b)	The preservation of the common interests of all Powers in China by insuring the independence and integrity of the Chinese Empire and the principle of equal opportunities for the commerce and industry of all nations in China;
(c)	The maintenance of the territorial rights of the high contracting parties in the regions of Eastern Asia and of India, and the defence of their special interests in the said regions.
I shall quote only two paragraphs from the body of the treaty. Articles II and IV are as follows:

If by reason of unprovoked attack or aggressive action, wherever arising, on the part of any Power or Powers, either high contracting party should be involved in war in defence of its territorial rights or special interests mentioned in the preamble of this Agreement, the other high contracting party will at once come to the assistance of its ally, and will conduct the war in common, and make peace in mutual agreement with it.

Should either high contracting party conclude a treaty of general arbitration with a third Power, it is agreed that nothing in this agreement shall entail upon such contracting party an obligation to go to war with the Power with whom such treaty of arbitration is in force.
Now, Great Britain or the British Empire did conclude a general treaty of arbitration with the United States-a treaty of arbitration that would fully comply with clause IV of the treaty. That particular treaty of arbitration, I understand, did not go into effect because of the failure of the United States Senate to ratify it. But subsequently, in 1914, a new argreement was entered into between
the United Kingdom and the United States with regard to the establishment of a peace commission. It was signed at Washington on September 15, 1914, and ratifications were exchanged at Washington on November 10, 1914. Article 1 of that treaty provides:
The high contracting parties agree that all disputes between them, of every nature whatsoever, other than disputes the settlement of which is provided for and, in fact, achieved under existing agreements between the high contracting parties, shall, when diplomatic methods of adjustment have failed, be referred for investigation and report to a Permanent International Commission, to be constituted in the manner prescribed in the next succeeding article; and they agree not to declare war or begin hostilities during such investigation and before the report is submitted.
I believe it is generally understood in Great Britain, that the treaty to which I have referred complies with Article 4 of the Anglo-Japanese treaty. A statement was recently issued by the Japanese ambassador in London, Baron Hayashi, to the effect that Japan recognized that any difference which might arise between the United States and Japan, if unfortunately such a difference did1 arise, Vvould not under the terms of the Anglo-Japanese treaty involve the British Empire. Therefore under the treaty as it now stands,
I do not believe there is any justification for the allegation that if a difference unfortunately did arise between Japan and the United States, the British Empire would be involved.
I do not believe there is justification for the criticism of this alliance which has been indulged in on the other side of the line. Japan has honourably carried out her obligations under the treaty, as has Great Britain, and there is no just ground for criticism of either. But, Mr. Speaker, that does not entirely end the matter. The Government of this country cannot ignore the feeling that does exist in the United States in reference to this alliance. I submit for the consideration of the Government the question whether it would not be found, after careful examination, that it is in the interest of good relations between the British Empire and the United States on the one hand and between Japan and the United States on the other, in the interests of good relations all round, that this treaty should not be renewed, at least in its present form. Not that we appreciate Japan less; but we want to be friends with every nation; we do not want any alliances that will prevent us from playing the part of friend to every nation in the world.

One word in conclusion in reference to the amendment moved by my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King). Mr. Speaker, I entirely concur in the views expressed by the Prime Minister and the leader of the Opposition, and also by the hon. member for King's, that we should endeavour in 'dealing with our inter-imperial affairs, and international relations, to avoid party differences and party conflicts. Up to this time every prime minister of Canada who has gone overseas has worthily represented our country no matter from which side of the House he has come. Canada has never had any reason to regret, the conduct of her prime minister while in London. On no occasion have her interests been sacrificed or prejudiced. I may not see eye to eye with the Prime Minister on all matters, but I believe that in this important matter the House and the country can obsolutely trust him just as they have trusted every prime minister of Canada in the past. The leader of the Opposition has heard the very clear statement of the Prime Minister. I do not share the view that we should seek to tie the hands of the Prime Minister at this conference. The Prime Minister has indicated what his line of action will be, so far, I think, as he could properly indicate it. What I regret most of all is that if my hon. friend presses his motion to a division there will be an appearance of difference in this House,-and that impression will be entertained in the country, in Great Britain and in other portions of the Empire, on matters in respect to which the House is not divided, but in respect to which all hon. members are substantially in agreement.

I would ask
my hon. friend this question: he has heard the statement I read this afternoon from the Prime Minister of England and also from the Colonial Secretary. I am sure he will agree that they are at variance with the statement made by the Prime Minister. How will the Prime Minister reconcile the position he will take at the conference with that of the Prime Minister of Great Britain if, for example, the Prime Minister of Great Britain holds to the attitude which he has set forth in the statement I have read to the House?

Well, Mr. Speaker, I
would say that the fundamental difference is this:	Other prime ministers are not
responsible to the parliament and the people of Canada; the Prime Minister of

Canada is. They are responsible to their own parliaments; he is responsible to this. He is not responsible for what they say; he is responsible for what he says and does. I am prepared, and I am sure this House is prepared-I believe my hon. friend is prepared-to believe that the Prime Minister of this country on these important matters, particularly in view of his statement to-day, can be trusted just as fully as other prime ministers in the past have been trusted to preserve and protect all Canadian interests while'seeking to promote the spirit of unity and hearty co-operation among all the states of the Empire.
I cannot close without making this appeal to my hon. friend, because of the great importance of the issue, because it affects not only our own position, but all portions of the Empire and our relations elsewhere. After hearing the statement of the Prime Minister and listening to the debate, I would urge my hon. friend to withdraw his amendment. Let us be unanimous in form as we are in fact on this question. On the first occasion on which the Government of Canada has taken the House into its confidence and asked the House to express its opinions freely on questions of great moment to the country, let us not divide the House when there is no division of opinion, but let us present a united front to the people of the Dominion, the people of the British Empire and the people of the other nations of the world.

Mr. Speaker, it may be for the convenience of the House, if in a very few words, I state, at this juncture, the view that is taken on the question before the House by the little group of members who sit in this corner. We had nothing to do with the arranging of the proposed conference and nothing to do with the drawing up of the amendment on going into Supply. But we are members of Parliament, and we have views about the merits of the amendment, which views we shall express in our vote if the matter goes to a vote.
In some words addressed to this House a few days ago, the Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) seemed to indicate that this conference, proposed to be held in June, was merely a preparatory conference. At that time, I formed the opinion that if it was merely a preparatory conference, and if practically no questions of concrete importance were to come before it, the preparation might very well go on for twelve months anyhow by correspondence, and that

it was a matter of doubtful expediency whether this conference should be held this year or not. I do not change from that view now. I would go a little further than the amendment does in its first clause in that respect. I would express a personal doubt about the value of this conference this year at all, on this ground first of all. Men's minds everywhere are yet so much in a state of flux that I very much question whether the world wants conferences at the present moment. We need to recall the events through which the world has passed during the last six or seven years, in which events we have so intimately participated. The conflict has been called a world-war, and well it might be. The Romanoffs have disappeared from the throne of Russia; the Hapsburgs have disappeared from the throne of Austria; the Hohenzollerns have disappeared from the throne of Germany, and Europe has been reduced to a state of practical chaos. For the first time in the history of the world, both hemispheres have been engaged in a conflict of unparalleled magnitude, and, as a result, the world's opinions are in a state of flux. Mankind is stunned into an apathetic condition, and when empires have been crumbling like this, I have the gravest doubt whether even the biggest men in the Empire cannot be better employed than meeting in London and embarking immediately upon a fresh scheme of empire building. That is my first remark in connection with this conference.
There are other reasons. Notwithstanding two recent by-elections, I think there is grave reason for doubting whether the Prime Minister of Britain represents the opinion of Britain at the present moment.
