Before the last two elections, opinion in that country was setting very steadily against the Prime Minister and his Government, and recent election results are probably due to the temporary cause of the labour upheaval. I have still grave doubt whether the Government of Canada at the present moment represents the opinion of Canada, and in its case there have been no by-elections to interfere with that doubt, because the by-elections have all gone in a particular direction. I feel perfectly certain that if our people from the Atlantic to the Pacific could be canvassed upon the simple question whether the greatest need of Canada in June is for her Prime Minister, after the unparallelled exertions which he has put forth in the House and out of it, since he became Prime Minister, to take part in a conference where subjects of great importance to the future of the world's peace and the future of the Empire are to be discussed and possibly put in the way of settlement, a large majority of our people would say:
" If that bright brain is not too tired, we would rather keep it at home to see if it cannot be better employed at the moment in helping to deal with Canadian problems, to relieve the unemployment situation, and to deal with other great problems that are concerning us in our own nation.'' For that matter, I think Mr. Hughes could find plenty to do in Australia along the same lines, and Mr. Winston Churchill and Mr. Lloyd George have, at the present moment, enough, in all conscience, on their hands in the British Isles to take a rest from foreign policy and from delicately manipulating the relations of the various portions of the Empire.
These remarks are based upon a supposition that this is a preparation conference for another bigger powwow to be held next year. I do not know why the hon. member for Durham (Mr. Rowell) is so enthusiastic to-night in favour of these successive powwows, because when he was in Geneva recently he told the people there that Canada could not afford to have her greatest men going across the Atlantic every year. I do not see that he is quite consistent in his view in that respect. If this conference is to be more than a preparatory conference, then I submit that there is no practical method of limiting the subjects that will come under discussion at it. Indeed, we have had evidence of that in the statements of the Prime Minister to-day. The other day his statement, if it had any meaning-and he generally makes his meaning pretty clear- seemed to be intended to lead the House to believe that this was to be a preparatory conference. But the moment he is met with a very carefully drawn resolution and a proposal that certain limitations of a very moderate kind should be put upon him,, under the influence of applause behind him, he grows, towards the end of his speech, as is his wont, quite combative, and seems to plead for an absolutely free hand to speak for Canada in his own right on any subject that may come before the conference of Prime Ministers. It is trut that he asked this House in one afternoon's debate to give him any counsel and direction which we felt we could give him. But he practically, in his closing remarks, in reply to my hon. friend the leader of

the Opposition, claimed a free hand in this matter.
Now may I draw attention for a moment to the wording of the amendment. It does not propose to limit those who go to that conference, if they do go, in regard to the matters they discuss. There is no proposal of that kind-no proposal of any limitation whatsoever as to discussion. It does state in very careful language certain principles which would limit action. Discussion is one thing, but action is a very different thing. So far as I can see, and I certainly do not need to follow my hon. friend from Durham over all possible subjects of inter-imperial and international disputes or discussion, there is only one question of concrete, practical importance upon which ostensibly my right hon. friend is proposing to go to London at all. I do not know whether my right hon. friend is going to be accompanied to London or not. It has been stated in the newspapers that my hon. friend the Minister of Marine (Mr. Ballantyne) is going with the Prime Minister. Well, I do not know that my hon. friend the Minister of Marine is an expert on Anglo-Japanese relations. He has not taken that question up yet. He will not take it up very long before he is very vigorous in his study of it, and before he becomes an expert, at least in his own mind. I said just now that if the people of this country were canvassed as to my right hon. friend going to London, I believed there would be a very large majority who would say that he could find better occupation at home. Now in regard to the Minister of Marine, I am perfectly sure that nine out of ten of our people, if they were asked whether he should go to Europe this summer, would say: " That is the minister-Is it not-who has a weakness for buying semi-obsolete war vessels and building unprofitable merchant ships? By all means keep him at home, for if he goes to Europe he will come back with a little flotilla of dreadnoughts behind him." However, that is by the way.
I was saying that in my judgment there is only one practical question upon which ostensibly the right hon. gentleman is going to London, and that is the Anglo-Japanese treaty. Now need that take my right hon. friend to London? This treaty is not being made for the first time. It was contracted, first, on behalf of the British Empire by the Marquis of Lansdowne many years ago, and I apprehend that when he made that treaty he would be in consultation with the Canadian Government of that day. The treaty was renewed by Sir Edward Grey,

now Viscount Grey, and I should be very much astonished to learn that that treaty was renewed by Sir Edward Grey without any communication with the Canadian Government. I do not know, but I think I should be making a good guess if I suggested that our Government has already had communications from the Imperial Government about the Anglo-Japanese treaty, and for the life of me I cannot see why an exchange of two or three despatches on each side should not make it perfectly plain to the Imperial Government what the mind of this Government is on the renewal or non-renewal of the Anglo-Japanese treaty. And that, according to my view, is about the only great subject that seems to be taking my right hon. friend to London at this time.
The Prime Minister in speaking on the amendment raised the point that it placed him under a restraint and-he argued that that was inadvisable because it was out of harmony with the principle of conference. He said the conference would be of no value at all if he went under the supposed restraint of the amendment. I do not see that that was well argued. The amendment does not mention conference or discussion. What it says in regard to alterations in the constitutional relationships between Canada and the Mother Country is that no steps should be taken to alter those relationships at the coming Conference. What it says on the other head, in regard to armaments, is not that discussion should not take place, but that no action should be taken committing Canada to enlarged expenditures of a military or naval nature at the present time. I cannot see in the wording of the amendment any attempt to restrain discussion whatsoever. Might I ask my right hon. friend if he contemplates the possibility of any change in the constitution of the British Empire at the coming conference in June? I am quite sure he does not. Might I ask him-I scarcely need to ask him-if he contemplates entering into any obligations whatsoever in the month of June to increase the naval and military expenditures of Canada at this time? He said in his speech, in effect, that he did not. Then, if he contemplates no change in the constitutional relationships, and if he contemplates taking no step to commit us to further obligations in regard to increased expenditure on armaments, whether by land or by sea, why does he not accept the amendment? That is the simple position in regard to it.

My hon. friend from Durham has pleaded for unity upon this question. The Government can get it in a moment, and get it in a way that would not be in the slightest degree derogatory to my right hon. friend and his Government. My right hon. friend has in effect, in his speech put himself under the very restraint which he complains of the amendment placing upon him, because he expressed the opinion in regard to armaments that we should take no steps in regard to them until the general question of armaments was discussed. That point has been emphasized and endorsed by my hon. friend from Durham. In other words, he accepts the principle of the amendment, yet proposes to vote it down. I cannot understand what his attitude of mind is if that is not it. Not only did he say in effect that he did not propose to have any increase of armaments at the present time, but he admitted that it would be a serious matter if any opinion were expressed at the conference or any view taken there by the Prime Minister in conflict with the views of the majority of the people of this country. Well, that is just the fear that evidently operated upon the minds of those who drew this very reasonable and carefully worded amendment, and I repeat, I cannot for the life of me see why the Government does not accept it.
We have heard a great deal about foreign policy. My own feeling is that this country and the world have had all the foreign policy they wantior a number of years. I recall that Mr. Gladstone, speaking on a memorable occasion, reminded his audience that the famous Greek Pericles had said that a man in relation to his wife was better off when he did not know he had one. Gladstone said that he was not quite prepared to endorse the proposition of Pericles in regard to the possession of a wife, but he said: "I am absolutely sure of this, that a country is in a far better position in regard to its foreign policy when it does not know it h.as one." Yet we have had a whole afternoon, after we have certainly had our fill of foreign policy for the last seven years, devoted to a discussion of the question how we can multiply and complicate the obligations of this country in the direction of Empire building. I consider that the step is ill taken and uneneeessary at this time, because, as I have said, the world has had its fill of foreign policy. There would indeed be nothing more serious than that my right hon. friend should express opinions or commit himself to views at that conference that were out of harmony with the views of the majority of the people of this country.
I assuredly think that the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), was well within his rights when he claimed for his amendment that it is not framed in any partisan spirit. I do not think there is any evidence of partisanship in the amendment at all. Not only is it not framed in the interests of party, but it is framed with the evident desire to help the Government in taking a stand which is for the good of this country and which is in harmony with the views of the great majority of the Canadian people, if I can form any judgment upon that point. Not only so, Mr. Speaker, but the amendment is framed in support of views which make for the peace, the progress and the happiness of mankind; and my right hon. friend will be well advised if he studies the amendment thoroughly, even after he has voted it down, and gets his system permeated with the principles that are contained in it.
We forget the events of yesterday. I remember very well that when I was supporting the Military Service Act in this House, I made the statement that we, like President Wilson, were in the war because we believed it was a war to end wars. Speaking for myself and those associated with me, I said that we were supporting conscription because we believed that this war would end conscription. And both sentiments were cheered t6 the echo by every hon. gentleman sitting opposite to me to-night. Those sentiments were received with cheers in the debate on the second reading of the Conscription Bill. Have we forgotten that those were the high ideals with which we went into the war? Have we forgotten that it was for those ideals that we lost 60,000 of the fairest and finest of Canadian manhood? Have we forgotten all these things when we so easily take up this question of Empire building once more and give another example of those who forget also the Scripture which says: "The eyes of the fool are in the ends of the earth"? Mr. Speaker, we can well afford to take a rest in this matter of armaments; we can well afford to rest for awhile from artificial Empire building.
What does the amendment assert? It asserts that those who vote for it are eminently satisfied with the British Empire as it is; and they are supported in that view by the fact that the Empire has come through such a strain as it was never

subjected to in its history, such a strain as no one expected that it would have to bear. It has come through with its flag flying at the top of its mast; the free Empire of Britain and her outlying Dominions. That Empire has emerged from the test in a most magnificent way, and what do we want to be doing with it? I say, give it a rest from this Empire building. How are you going to make it better? Do you expect to strike another war next week bigger than the one we have been through? There is no need for these things at the present time; there is no need for thinking of increasing armaments. The amendment asserts that we are satisfied with the Empire as it is. It asserts that what the world wants is rest; what the world wants is honest industrial occupation; what weary men and women want is more fresh air, if you like, but not more Empire building, and certainly not more armaments.
What were the objects held out to us throughout the whole of the war? What were we fighting for? It was said: Reparation shall be made to Belgium and France more than they have lost. This was the statement of Mr. Asquith which was taken up in every portion of the Empire and of the Allied countries. The Hapsburgs and Hohenzollerns, many of us asserted, would pass from their thrones; and these predictions have been fulfilled. It was declared that never again would another nation break international law without the knowledge that all civilized races of mankind would be against it the moment the breach was made, and that, following an understanding of the civilized nations to that effect, steps should be taken towards a large measure of general disarmament. If my right hon. friend were going into a conference to commence working night and day, declaring that Canada was in the forefront of leadership in a movement to bring about that disarmament, then I should say, "by all means, go to the conference". But there are doubts in our minds; there are fears that there may be commitments made along certain lines. We propose, therefore, so far as this corner of the House is concerned, I think, unanimously, to support the amendment, because, in our soul and conscience, we support two propositions which it contains as being propositions which we believe to be held by the great majority of the people of this country, propositions which make for the progress, the happiness, the prosperity of mankind, and which alone, if carried out, can bring to a weary

humanity the things for which we asserted we are fighting all the time the war was on.

I
wish simply to make two or three remarks in connection with the long debate which we have had on a most important question. It is rather difficult for me to see why the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) has proposed this motion, but it is still more difficult for me to follow the arguments of some gentlemen who have spoken in support of it. The member for. Gaspe and Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) has given us a very ornate speech in reference to a great many things-ancient history as well as modern-but he has not strongly and appositely devoted himself to the proposition that was laid down bj the leader of the Opposition. Amongst the other speeches-which have been of a high order if I may be allowed to express an opinion-we have heard a speech from the member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark). It had a great many excellent things in it but it seems to me to have gone a good deal wide of the mark.
Let us take just two or three sample observations on the question. If there was anything in the argument of my hon. friend from Red Deer, it was that there should not be a conference at all, or at least that the Prime Minister had better stay at home and not attend the conference. Th at was driven home with a good deal of force. But we are up against a fact. The fact is that a conference has been determined upon and that it will be held, that the other Overseas Dominions have arranged for their premiers to attend it, and some of them are now on the way. What is the use of getting up here and making a drive at the uselessness, so to speak, of the conference when the Mother Country and the Overseas Dominions have decided that there should be one when it has been called, and it will take place? If we must be consistent we must be prepared to say that that conference can go on, that it can be carried through, that it may have the premiers of all the other Overseas Dominions, but that Canada would be wise to keep out of it entirely. I do not think the people of Canada, I do not think this House, is disposed to ask that Canada shall take that position with reference to this conference. For my part I would not think it would be wise to do so and to say that as the conference had better not be attended by Canada. I do not think that such an attitude is within the running,

unless we are prepared to state that we will sit by and see a conference carried on with the co-operation of all the other Overseas Dominions and the Mother Country, but that we shall not be present, or be heard, at that conference.
Take the other point of view. I have followed very closely the discussions which have taken place in the other Overseas Dominions, and I cannot find that either there, or at home, there has been any attempt on the part of the legislatures or parliaments of those countries to bind or tie the hands of their representatives by the passage of a resolution; in all cases they will be there and will have gone with the confidence of their parliaments and their legislatures behind them. What is the reason we should act differently from these other Dominions and imply lack of confidence in the representative who goes to take Canada's part in that conference? We might go back in Canadian history a little -it has been mentioned already, it is no harm to mention it again-and during all the years from 1894 until the present time that we have had these gatherings-at first Intercolonial Conferences, and then these other conferences resulting in the Imperial Conference of the last ten or fifteen years -on no single occasion, as far as my memory goes, has there been any attempt on the part of the House to hamper in any possible way the Prime Minister who went to those conferences. When Sir Wilfrid Laurier went over to attend those conferences he went as Prime Minister. Between him and the Opposition in the House there were strong divergencies of opinion-much stronger divergencies of opinion than exist to-day between hon. gentlemen opposite and the present Prime Minister-and yet there was no occasion on which the Opposition tried in the least to impute a lack of confidence in him as Prime Minister of Canada, or to send him over with bonds and shackles about him. Why should it be done in this instance? But there is an additional reason 10 p.m. why it is not necessary, and that is afforded by the admissions of my hon. friends themselves. As already stated, on no previous occasion, prior to the departure of our prime ministers to attend these conferences, has there been a full and free opportunity given for discussion with an invitation for suggestions and advice, and, in a way for instruction. This time the opportunity has been afforded, and the Prime Minister to-day, and in his previous utterances, has stated
the course that he proposed to follow at the approaching conference. That statement of his agrees absolutely with the propositions that have been put forward in the speeches of hon. gentlemen who have already spoken to-day, and agrees exactly with the two main propositions in the amendment which the leader of the Opposition has proposed. If, under these circumstances, the Prime Minister has stated that he does not propose to bind this Parliament or this country by any conclusions of a concrete nature, and if hon. gentlemen believe the Prime Minister's assertion, as they say they do, why is there any necessity for moving this amendment? If it is not necessary to restrain impetuous and reckless desire to commit this country, what is the use of it? If there had been any indication of such, a desire there might have been some ground assumed for passing such a resolution. As there has not been, why is the resolution necessary, on the admission of the members themselves who have spoken that-the Prime'Minister has frankly and fully stated that he does not propose to assent to any concrete conclusions which shall bind this country?
If those are arguments on one side, there is to my mind an argument on the other side that is more powerful still. I say it with all becoming moderation, but I doubt myself if it is for the interest and the reputation of Canada that, after the statement her Prime Minister has made of the lines which he has laid down, Canada should send him to that conference with a divided sentiment in this House behind him, such divided sentiment being based upon what? Upon the simple idea that the House, so far as the Opposition was concerned, did not trust the word of the Prime Minister, and did not believe that he ought to go without these shackles about him. I do not think that is going to contribute to the reputation and dignity of Canada, and I am quite certain that it puts our representative in an individious position compared with the representatives of all the other parts of the Empire who will attend that conference. I do not want to use too harsh a word, but I do not think it is a seemly position for our House of Commons to take under the circumstances, and I should be very sorry to see it taken. I had it in mind-my hon. friend from Durham (Mr. Rowell) made the proposition himself-that if I said anything at all tonight after this discussion had proceeded on the line it has, I would suggest that it would be proper and advantageous for my

hon. friend to withdraw his amendment. I am not sure whether he will or not. He may think now there is some advantage to be gained by pressing it to a vote, but I am quite certain that when he thinks it over in his cooler moments he will see that he has pressed a matter which has not been quite in accordance with the necessities of the case, nor with the dignity of this House. I shall be sorry if he presses his resolution to a vote, but that is for him and his associates to settle for themselves.
Now, when you come down really to the matter before us, what is it that this Parliament does hold in its hands? It is the absolute right to be the final arbiter of any conclusions which may be arrived at at these conferences-this conference or the conference which is to succeed it next year. The whole purpose of this conference is not to come to conclusions in the concrete. It has a purpose quite as important as that which is the purpose of next year's conference. I am not one who feels that we ought to speak slightingly about a preparatory conference looking to a conference of much greater moment in a way which is to take place next year. 1 am not so cocksure as my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) that you can settle all these things to the greatest advantage by sending a despatch or two across the Atlantic and getting an answer back. If there is anything that distinguishes the work of the world to-day it is the willingness of its representative men to sit down around a common table and to exchange views with reference to the great interests which are confided to their charge. That is shown in the world's history of the last ten or fifteen years, and never to a greater extent than now. If there is one influence to-day which is working for a better understanding, and consequently for peace, it is the idea of a system of conferences between men of all grades of public merit and importance. And in these conferences where men meet together in conversation, in question and answer, in the putting forth of opinion and reply, and the canvass thereto they get at common views, and they are enabled to do their work much better. Undoubtedly it is an influence which is of untold benefit in working for the good understanding which is necessary to world peace.
My hon. friend from Red Deer says that we have had enough of foreign policies and of foreign countries during the last seven or eight years. Well, we have had a good

deal of them, and we have had a lot of world-work to do. But those foreign countries still exist; international interests still exist; inter-imperial interests still exist, and to my mind there are many things which require at this very day conference and understanding not only between the public men of various countries, but between the public men who have to do with the Empire itself. Readjustment of the work of the future, getting together for mutual understanding, are as necessary now as they were during the war, and to my mind a preparatory conference which takes into account the big and important questions, the questions upon which the weal or woe of this Empire depends to a very large extent, cannot be canvassed too soon by men from different parts of the Empire meeting together and going into close and intimate conference with reference to them.
It is all very well on a call of a month or two next year when the Imperial Conference meets to go to London to settle the big questions which we all admit are to be settled in some way there; that is one thing; but it is a mighty sight more important to get the benefits of personal conference first and then have the advantage of a year to think over and to pursue those personal conferences before you come up against the actual concrete solution of those big questions which will be before us within the next two years. Surely I am right there, surely it is not a waste of time that Canada should send her Prime Minister for that purpose in order that he may bring back to those who are his colleagues next year that intimate knowledge which can only be gained from these personal conferences with the heads of the Empire one with another next June.
I am rather surprised that men should think, and actually argue upon the thought, that no previous consideration should be given along the lines I have laid down; that nothing of that kind should take place until the Imperial Conference is convened, and that then in a fortnight or three weeks you should be called upon, in the rush of those busy hours, to come to your conclusions. My mind is that it is the part of wisdom to have this Conference of Prime Ministers now, to get at the. information, to get the views of representatives of other parts of the Empire. Then those who attend the conference may, upon that information and that interchange of opinions, bring back to the councils of their respective countries their views with regard to the matters dis-

cussed; the whole situation can he canvassed and re-canvassed-as would not be possible through the medium of letter or despatch writing-in the light of the living and intimate knowledge thus obtained of the various questions considered. This done, when next year the Imperial Conference is called, with its admittedly big questions to consider, we shall be glad to send our men there in the best possible manner fitted for the work which they will be called upon to do. I again urge upon my hon. friend, therefore, that it would be the part of wisdom for him to withdraw his resolution.
I think that in this matter we should proceed along historic lines-that is one argument. I think it should be done as is suggested because a Parliament should always have faith in its Prime Minister; when he outlines his work and pledges himself to a course of conduct, Parliament should accept his statement, should take his word and give him its confidence. Parliament should not embody in a shackling resolution what, if the word of the Prime Minister can be relied upon, is not necessary, and what carries with it a division in this House, an implication that the Prime Minister goes across with what might be called a divided confidence so far as the House is concerned-that Canada is not speaking as a whole. Now, that is simply the way it strikes me. We are not going over there, in the person of our Prime Minister, to meet enemies; we are going over to counsel with friends. To listen to some of the remarks which have been made here this afternoon, one would think that the Prime Minister was going over to put his head into a den of robbers- men who wanted to take advantage of him and of this country; who'wanted to draw us into intrigues and into conclusions which would be disadvantageous to Canada and to the Empire as a whole.

Who suggested a den
of robbers?

Why, my hon.
friend himself. Of course, he did not use the word "robbers."	[DOT]
Grossly exaggerated.

But threequarters of the speech of my hon. friend from Maisonneuve, if he will allow me to say it, was of a somewhat mischevious nature. It bred suspicion; it breathed suspicion; it played upon prejudice, as my hon. friend knows how to play upon prejudice.
He had to say something with reference to Winston Churchill. What good on earth or under heaven could come from allusion in debating a question of this kind to something that Winston Churchill might have said years ago or might not have said years ago?

Said it against the
right hon. gentleman in England.

Why should
the hon. member for Maisonneuve drag in the Round Table again, as though the Round Table formulated the policies of this Government? My hon. friend loves that bogey. He has slept with it for the last ten years. It is a bogey which, when he pulls the string, may do some good to him in certain particulars and respects. But I must say to my hon. friend that he is capable of much better than that. He has an Imperial tendency as well, and I commend him for it. Why on earth should he bring out these breeders of suspicion, these arousers of prejudice, in the discussion of a question like this? I say again that we are not going over to Great Britain in the person of the Prime Minister to alight amongst enemies

those who wish to take advantage of Canada, to rope her into something egregious, something against her interests. I do not look at it in that way, neither does my hon. friend, in his heart. He has time and again in this House traced the evolution of the constitutional liberties of Great Britain and of the parts of the Empire which, as Overseas Dominions, are closely united to her. He has done it with his usual eloquence and his usual ability. Never in the history of that evolution has there been on the part of English statesmen a desire to take any action as affecting Canada or the other Overseas Dominions which is not fair and square and honest and for the benefit of the Empire as a whole. As a matter of fact, nothing can be done to bind this Parliament until the measures are brought back and laid before this Parliament. My hon. friend says: Then why not pass the resolution? Well, why not add a codicil to your resolution? Why not lay down just the cut of the clothes that the Prime Minister shall wear when he goes to that conference? The Prime Minister gives us to understand that he will go very well clothed; but my hon. friend says:	Then,
why not have it put in a resolution that he shall go well clothed? The Prime Minister says: I do not propose to do this and to do that, or come to any concrete

conclusions. Then why is it necessary to put it in a resolution? My argument against the resolution is founded upon its uselessness and its mischievousness. I would rather see it withdrawn and I would like to prevail, if I could, upon my hon. friend to make it better for Canada, better for himself in his after reflections, better for his peace of conscience, by saying: We believe the Prime Minister's assertion; he has frankly laid down his policy and his proposed -line of conduct; we trust him and we shall put no shackles about him.

Mr. Speaker, the arguments which my right hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) has adduced in support of his suggestion that the motion of the hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) be withdrawn do not impress me very deeply. My right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) stated this afternoon that while he could not accept the amendment of the hon. leader of the Opposition, he was quite willing to accept suggestions from the members of the House as to the stand he should take on the various matters to be discussed at the coming conference. If individual members of the House are invited to offer suggestions, what is the harm on the part of the whole House in offering a suggestion by way of a resolution? If an individual suggestion is invited, why should a collective suggestion be refused? The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) says that this would be a shackle, and that it is a lack of dignity on the part of this Parliament to offer such a motion. My opinion as to that differs from that of my right hon. friend. Is there any lack of dignity on the part of Parliament in expressing its opinion on questions which vitally affect the future of Canada? Is there any lack of dignity on the part of the House of Commons in giving its opinion, in making an assertion of what it believes oh questions which are very important for our country? The trouble is that this Government has developed the habit of ruling in an arbitrary way by Orders in Council, as it has done so frequently, ignoring altogether Parliament and its prerogatives and rights. The people of this country to-day want the prerogatives and rights of Parliament restored, and they will certainly approve the resolution presented by the leader of the Opposition, especially when there is in that resolution nothing which opposes anything set forth by the 
Prime Minister or any other hon. gentleman on the other side.
My right hon. friend says that this amendment is not in harmony with the principle of a conference. Why not? Why, I repeat, is a collective suggestion by Parliament not in harmony with the principle of a conference? Why should the expression of a mandate to our representative at that conference hamper his action there? It is true, as my right hon. friend has stated, that any decision reached at the conference shall have to be approved by the Parliament of Canada before it is binding. But, Sir, I believe that we have a right to express our opinion before the discussion takes place at the conference. We have a right to tell our representatives what we want and what we do not want, and there is nothing in that which means derogation from the dignity of either Parliament or the gentleman who will represent Canada at that conference.
Having made this statement, I will proceed to examine very briefly the four matters which my right hon. friend says now will be submitted to that conference. The first is: Preparation for the special constitutional conference contemplated in resolution 9 of the Imperial War Conference of 1917. There is no objection to preparation for the holding of that conference. I am not sure whether it was necessary to hold a special meeting of Prime Ministers for that purpose. I am inclined to agree with the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) that correspondence would have brought about the same result. There is, however, no harm in that conference, and I quite agree that some system must be devised for the holding of that very important conference. May I suggest, in view of the fact that some hon. gentlemen have offered suggestions as to the date of that conference, that it should not be held prior to a general election in Canada. It is very important that the men who will represent Canada at that momentous gathering shall have the full support, if not of the whole population, at least of the majority of the people of the country.
They have that.
My hon. friend from Simcoe says that they have that support. Of course, he is not serious in that.
He is a trouble maker.

Yes. As to the other suggestion that men, representative of the various political groups in the Dominions,

should be invited to take part in the conference, perhaps that is a good idea, and I shall be glad indeed, so far as I am concerned, to see the right hon. gentleman present as leader of the Opposition in the Canadian House of Commons.
The second and the fourth matters which are suggested relate to foreign relations and to external affairs concerning all parts of the Empire. May I say that these two matters should be postponed until after the constitutional conference takes place? It is only after that constitutional conference shall have taken place that the real status of Canada shall be defined, and that the British Dominions shall know in a clear way the true and real nature of the political union between the various parts of the Empire. Then and then only, I suggest that we shall know whether it is in. the interest of Canada, whether it is opportune for Canada, to take part in the shaping of the foreign affairs of the Empire, and to what extent we should do that. Though I agree with much that has been stated by the hon. member for Durham (Mr. Rowell), especially as regards the principle upon which his arguments are based, I differ as to many methods which he has suggested, as to what will be involved, and what will he the interpretation and meaning of certain governmental activities. There is a danger in our country meddling too much in foreign affairs without any reservation. The hon. member for King's (Sir Robert Borden) quoted words of the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier, with which I am in full sympathy, concerning the gradual evolution of Canada in the course of the development of its autonomy. But while holding these views, the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier always objected to our country taking part in the discussions and decisions regarding the foreign affairs of the Empire. As late as in 1911, at the Imperial Conference, when Australia proposed a resolution of regret that the Dominions were not consulted prior to the acceptance by the British delegates of the terms of the Declaration of London Sir Wilfrid Laurier, speaking to the resolution, said:
That is a thing which, in my humble judgment, ought to be left altogether to the responsibility of the Government of the United Kingdom. Tou ought not to give advice unless you are prepared to back the advice with a'l your strength.
That is the danger which faces us when we have the ambition to offer our advice regarding the foreign affairs of the British
Empire. We cannot give our advice unless we are prepared, as my late hon. leader stated on that occasion, to back our advice with all our strength. I do not think that the people of Canada wish or are prepared to-day to say that they will put all the strength of the country or what is left of her resources, and all her manhood, behind any scheme concerning Prussia, Mesopotamia, or any other country with which the foreign affairs of the Empire may be concerned. My hon. friend the member for Durham did not always speak in very complimentary terms of European diplomacy, and I am surprised, therefore, that he is so anxious to have a part in that diplomacy.
I am sure that he does not suppose that our offering advice will cure all the evils he complains of. Speaking at Geneva last summer, my hon. friend said:
Fifty thousand Canadian soldiers under the sod in Europe is the price Canada has paid for the European statesmanship which drenchec the continent in blood.
Those words were the subject of much comment, but I may say that so far as I am concerned I admire the courage of my hon. friend in expressing his opinion in the way he did. But, Mr. Speaker, I do not see how he can reconcile that statement with his anxiety to take part in all the conferences and all the discussions which may lead to a decision concerning the foreign policy of the British Empire. Canada must go slowly along that line.
Does my hon. friend wish an answer to that question?
I am always pleased to listen to my hon. friend.

The answer is quite simple. In my judgment the world's peace can only be preserved by international cooperation to preserve it, by peaceful means, and that involves all nations coming in and doing their share. I think Canada should do her share with the other nations.

I do not see how our giving advice to the British Foreign Office will lead to bringing that about. It is because I am afraid of taking the responsibility which our advice in every such case involves that I did not approve of some of the conditions in arrangement concerning the appointment of a Minister Plenipotentiary to Washington, though at the time I approved of almost everything my right hon. friend from King's (Sir Robert Borden) and my hon. friend from Durham stated. The feature which I do not like is

that our representative at Washington shall act for the British Ambassador in his absence. If the representative of Canada acts for the United Kingdom or for the British Empire on such occasions, I do not see how we can escape responsibility for his actions. He will be our nominee, appointed upon the advice of Canadian ministers. I do not like that feature of the appointment which makes him British Ambassador as well as Canadian representative at Washington.
The third subject which is referred to is the Anglo-Japanese Alliance. As far as that is concerned, I do not see why we should send a representative to London to discuss the matter with the representatives of the United Kingdom. What I suggested this afternoon while the right hon. the Prime Minister was speaking, I suggest again to-night, and that is the insertion of a clause in the treaty-such a clause was inserted in the British-French War Treaty, upon the request, I am sure, of my hon. friend from King's who was then Prime Minister-stipulating that the treaty should not be binding upon Canada unless and until it has been approved by the Canadian Parliament. That would safeguard Canada's rights; there would then be no danger for Canada. We have no business to tell the United Kingdom not to enter into a war treaty with Japan so long as the treaty will not affect us unless we wish it to do so. I think our representative at the conference should insist that the treaty, if it is renewed, shall be ratified by the Parliament of Canada. Then it will be time for us to consider whether or not we should enter into that alliance. The position of Canada in that respect is a delicate one. I wish to be perfectly frank about it. A famous English writer has said that a diplomat is an honest man who goes abroad to lie for his country, but we are so young in diplomacy that we can afford to tell the truth. Mr. Speaker, the conditions that existed in 1911 when the Anglo-Japanese treaty was made do not exist to-day. I think everybody will agree with me that at that time it was against Russia that Japan was seeking protection, and possibly Germany, but no such danger exists to-day. The only possible war 

and I trust to God that such a disaster shall be scared humanity-would be one with the United States, and I am not sure that Canada should bind herself to an alliance which would compel her to fight against that country in any struggle with Japan. At least, it is a question that involves 
great difficulties and one that ought to be considered very seriously by the people of Canada and by this Parliament before we give our consent to any treaty of that nature.
As to the rest of the agenda, my right hon. friend the Prime Minister says that the time at the disposal of the conference will be limited and that it is quite probable that these subjects will not be discussed; and, indeed, he intimates that the question of naval defence shall not be considered at the conference. My right hon. friend the member for King's (Sir Robert Borden), and my hon. friend from Durham, as also hon. gentlemen on the other side, have emphasized that this is not the time for Canada to increase her armaments, either naval or otherwise. Well, it is all very well for hon. gentlemen to say this, and I am very much pleased with all these statements that have been made this afternoon and to-night. I do not forget, however, that the first statement of the Prime Minister on March 4 indicated that the main question was that of naval policy based upon the principle of co-operation. This question and the Anglo-Japanese Treaty were stated as being the subjects to be discussed. I must not forget, either, that in the British House of Commons, as well as in statements made by public men in the United Kingdom, it has been asserted that the whole question of military and naval defence will be discussed and even decided at the forthcoming conference in June. My right hon. friend says, and I am pleased to hear the statement, that no action shall be taken with regard to naval defence. Well, what is the harm in having it stated in a resolution that would strengthen the hands of the Prime Minister? This resolution only indicates that the Parliament of Canada is at one with the Government in refusing to discuss naval defence this year, and my right hon. friend, instead of being weakened by this assertion on the part of Parliament, would be strengthened, in refusing to be drawn into a discussion of that question. The right hon. member for King's and other gentlemen who have spoken on this phase of the question have declared that we should wait until a scheme of disarmament is decided upon as between the various nations of the world. This is a very good reason indeed in support of the contention that any such discussion should be postponed. But there is the financial side of the question, which is mentioned in this resolution presented by my hon. friend the

leader of the Opposition; and there is the other all-important argument that nothing of this kind should be done until the Constitutional Conference has defined what is our status in the British Empire. Then and only then shall we know exactly to what scheme of defence, naval or otherwise, we would commit ourselves, and it is only after that conference has taken place and its findings have been approved by this Parliament, as well as by the other parliaments of the Empire, that any general scheme of naval defence should be entered upon.
There is only one thing more I wish to mention, and that is the fact that this conference, as my right hon. friend and the member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark), have pointed out, is to be a meeting of Prime ministers. I do not see why any other member of the Cabinet should go to London to attend this conference of Prime Ministers. We have only one Prime Minister, and we need all our ministers in this country at the present time. There are very grave and serious problems to settle, and it has been a source of dissatisfaction and of complaint throughout Canada that for the last two years our ministers have been spending more time abroad than they have devoted to the consideration of domestic problems in Canada. If the Prime Minister must go, let him go; but we love our other ministers so much that w'e want to keep them with us.
In conclusion, I want to ask hon. members: why should this amendment be opposed? The amendment merely asserts that, in the opinion of this House, no constitutional change in our relations with the Empire should be decided upon at this conference. Well, that is the general opinion as expressed in this House. This is not to be a constitutional conference; it is only a meeting of prime ministers. Every one agrees with that part of the amendment. Then, why vote against it? The other part of the amendment is the assertion that no action should be taken with regard to increasing expenditures on naval or military affairs. Every one, including the Prime Minister, has suggested that this discussion should not take place. Why, therefore, refuse to accept the amendment, which merely embodies these two principles that are accepted by all the members of the House, including members of the Government? I say, Mr. Speaker, that Parliament does well to express its definite opinion as to what should take place at this conference. Parliament does well to give a
mandate to its representative. Before he goes to that conference he should have the authority to speak for the Canadian people. Canada has a right to specify what she wants him to state there, so far as policies are concerned; and reciprocating the invitation put forward by my right hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster), who has asked us to withdraw the amendment, I invite him to support it.

At this late hour I have no desire to prolong the debate. I merely wish to express a few sentiments in regard to the amendment and to the question before the House which I believe have so far been overlooked. I followed with a great deal of interest the recital by various speakers during the debate of the growth of the constitution of this country. After listening to the hon. member for Maisonneuve and Gaspe (Mr. Lemieux) one would reach the conclusion that the development of the constitution of Canada was not a matter of easy and smooth growth, but that it came out of a struggle for existence, a struggle for liberty from beginning to end. In the historical works of Canada and in the writings of many of our public men that view of the situation is given, but to my mind it is a very wrong one. Great Britain has a history in regard to colonial government extending back for four hundred years. Any one who has studied the history of the colonies of British America, now the United States, will get a much clearer view of the status of Canada, and the constitutional growth of the Dominion, than they will by listening to a lot of talk about what Lord Durham did, and what Lord So and So. said of Canada, forty or fifty years ago. The colonial office in England has a history and there they know how to deal with colonial affairs-they have had a great deal of experience. The American colonies had much wider scope and had greater autonomy than Canada has to-day, but that did not prevent civil war and the breaking away of those colonies from the Mother Land. They wrote their own charters and in the case of two or three of the colonies-such as New Jersey, I think, and [DOT] Pennsylvania and Carolina-they selected their own governors which we have never done. Now what was the reason, the fundamental reason, why there was a break between those colonies and the Mother Land? We must follow the history of the colonial system in what is now the United

States if we are going to arrive at any conclusion as far as our own colonial system, so-called, is concerned. The American colonies assisted Great Britain in her wars against the French and Spaniards. They sent 5,000 men to Carthagena with General Vernon. In the war between France and England they manned a large number of warships to fight against the French, and they carried on in exactly the same way as Canada is carrying on now. What was the reason that trouble arose? Inside of virtually twenty years after the French had been swept from this continent trouble arose between the colonies and the Mother Country. The reason was that no effort was made to bring about a meeting between th'e principal leaders of thought and of politics in those colonies and the leaders of thought and politics in Great Britain. There was no interchange of ideas; there were no conferences of premiers such as are taking place now. The colonies drifted away from the Mother Land, and it took very little irritation of a local character to bring about a break between England and her colonies whereby those colonies were lost. In discussing this question as to what we are going to do, and what the position of Canada is to-day in the Empire, we should look very carefully over what happened over a hundred years ago. By doing that and studying the question seriously we may arrive at a sensible conclusion now.
In regard to the forthcoming conference the Prime Minister has made a statement and taken Parliament into his confidence, something that has never occurred in the history of these gatherings in England. The right hon. gentleman has said that he is going over as one of the prime ministers of the Overseas Dominions to take part in the discussion of affairs over there. He has recited to the House the various points and the various matters which are to be discussed there, and he has assured the House that, as far as he is concerned, if there is any conclusion to be arrived at he will first submit the question to the House before coming to any definite decision on the subject. I have a recollection of previous conferences in England which have been attended by Canadian Prime Ministers and I have never yet seen one of them take the House into his confidence as the present Prime Minister has done. I think that Parliament should reciprocate and not try in any manner 11 p.m. to bind his hands. Now the subjects that will come up
[Mr Currie.]
there for discussion and settlement are really of great importance to us. Whilst the war has ceased there is the question as to arms and armament in future. Then there is no doubt that a great industrial war is taking place at the present time, and the position of Great Britain and her Dominions from a commercial and industrial point of view will no doubt come, up for discussion at that conference. To my mind there are several matters that should be considered. For instance, I think that the question of banking should be discussed by the Prime Minister at that conference. At the present time the Empire .is really at war financially. There are no credits between the various colonies and Great Britain and Canada, and something should be done that will smooth over the question of banking and the question of exchange as far as the British Dorriinions are concerned, so that we can carry on business with a reasonable measure of success. If there had been a conference last year, if there had not been such a disposition on the part of some hon. gentlemen opposite to prevent any consultation between the Government of this country and the Government of Great Britain last year, if the leader of the agricultural group had not opposed the question of dealing with unite instead of dealing with the whole of Europe on the subject of grain, I am quite satisfied that this country would have been at least a hundred millions better off than it is to-day. Then there is the question as to trade between foreign countries and the members of the British Empire. These, and other matters will have to be discussed.
Coming back to the resolution and the reasons advanced in its favour, that resolution is an astonishing one to me. I never saw a move of this kind in the House before, and I am very much surprised at the attitude of the Agrarian group in respect to it. In their platform, and in their policy, the Agrarian group have certainly come out very strongly in favour of British connection. They have come out very strongly in support of trade with Great Britain. They want us to have reciprocal trade with Great Britain, they want a greater preference' accorded Great Britain, and they want free trade with Great Britain in four or five years from now. Still they are going to support a resolution which is designed to prevent the Prime Minister of this country from going over to talk over anything of that kind with the British Government. I think that is a wrong attitude for them to take.

I think it is an anti-British attitude, if f may be allowed fo so characterize it. If I were asked to point out the object of this resolution I would simply say that it seeks to tie the hands of the Prime Minister who has clearly informed the House that it is not his intention to do anything that would impose any burdens on Canada, or would lead to any closer union than now exists in the British Empire. I do not think it is possible for us to be brought by any human agency into any closer union than now prevails. It is not a written constitution that will bring about closer relations within the Empire. Written constitutions are like the harness on a horse; it is not the harness that draws the load, it is the animal itself. When war broke out with Germany nobody stopped to discuss whether under the constitution we were called upon to supply our quota of troops, and if the same issue arose tomorrow we would do just the very same as we did in 1914. It is not a written constitution that is of any value to us- it is the feeling of good will and the desire for amicable relations between its component parts that is going to unite the Empire more closely.
Mention has been made of Mesopotamia, and it has been said that we must not do this or do that. Now what is the trouble in regard to Mesopotamia? The great Standard Oil Company in the United States -and I suppose the leader of the Opposition might be able to give us a little clearer knowledge of the facts-acting through the United States Government, stated that they do not want Great Britain to take the Mesopotamia oil fields and that Great Britain's mandate for that territory must virtually cease. As a matter of fact, the mandate of Great Britain in .Mesopotamia has ceased to function, there is no credit, and thousands of dollars worth of goods are lying on the wharves to the great loss of British traders. I do not see why Great Britain or the Dominions should exercise themselves very much as to the views of other countries regarding their attitude; the Mother Country and her Dominions are large enough and strong enough to carry on in their own way. For my part, I am quite satisfied that when our Prime Minister goes to England he will be able to take his place alongside of any of the so-called diplomats from the various parts of the Empire, that there is not very much danger of their gold-bricking him, and that he will keep out of three card monte and other games of
chance. To my mind this is a most foolish resolution-
Order.

Yes; and I cannot understand how any person who is a believer in British connection, who loves his country and is proud of the part she has taken in the war, and who looks forward to the future peace and prosperity of the Empire could assume the attitude which this resolution really suggests-that Canada does not wish to take any further part in the affairs of the Empire, and that we will not trust our Prime Minister to attend the conference in June. That is really what this resolution means.
A short time ago South Africa voted on the question whether that country should remain in the Empire, but her people saw the light and they returned Smuts and his party with an overwhelming majority, and that part of the Empire is now secure within the fold. We all appreciate what the people of South Africa are doing to build up that great country, and it is a pleasure to know that they are succeeding beyond their wildest dreams. The credit of South Africa is first class, in fact much better than that of Canada, and they are rapidly building up their banking and financial institutions. Their Prime Minister will be at this conference. The great Commonwealth of Australia lately debated the question whether Premier Hughes should have a free hand at the conference, and in spite of the fact that he has only a very narrow majority the House gave him an overwhelming vote of confidence. This country is looked upon as the brightest gem in the crown of Empire, she is always regarded as likely to achieve something great in Empire affairs, and the Prime Minister as her representative at the conference should have a free hand. A great deal of discussion has taken place about the Japanese Treaty and the difficulties between that country and the United States. I feel confident that if there is anything that will obviate war and assure continued peace between those two countries it is the attitude of Canada in regard to that treaty. It would be a very grave mistake for us to tie our hands. There may be some difficulties in the way, but the peace attitude on that whole question is the Canadian attitude, and our views should prevail. Why tie the hands of our Prime Minister in any way? As I have said before the resolution is one which cannot appeal

to any member with British sentiments. It is virtually an anti-British resolution.
Oh, oh.

Yes, it kicks the props from under our British connection. We might' as well look upon it as it really! is, and then every man will know what he is voting for. To vote for this resolution is to vote want of confidence not only in our own Prime Minister but in the Prime Ministers of Great Britain and our sister Dominions. That is the true attitude behind this resolution, and if its sponsors want to force it on the House, why, we will all know how to vote.

The two Australian Parliaments have passed an Act providing for a tax of $500 upon every Oriental immigrant, but that legislation was disallowed by a Foreign Office through the Governor General, of Australia, notwithstanding the fact that she is a sister nation standing on the same footing as the other nations within the Empire. Since that time, Australia has endeavoured to collect, through her agents, the tax to which the Japanese object, as they feel they have the support of Downing Street. Since then Great Britain did not hesitate to enter into a treaty with Japan. This is how the situation is described by an American correspondent:-
Australians will not have any Japanese for the same reason that California is rejecting them. The only way for the British Government is to make a new alliance, which instead of dealing with Japan, will protect the British interests in the East, and Australians believe that the future of the United States in the East will compel the Mother Country to follow their policy.
We see, however, the two allied countries arming themselves through mutual distrust. Admiral Falks, who is in command of the British squadron in Asia states that he could not give battle in eastern waters because there is no proper naval base there. It would be foolish, he says, to try and defend Australia at such a great distance from our naval base. Should a ship be . damaged, we would have to go back to Great Britain for important repairs. However, Great Britain is having a powerful naval base built up at Singapore with a very large dry-dock. On the other hand the Japanese are establishing a naval base on the Marshall islands. And the Americans are constantly urging the advantage of England making use of the dry-dock at Pearl harbour in connection with her base at Singapore.
English statesmen are of the opinion that Japan needs an outlet to her surplus population; they are building up their navy on a larger scale than the United States; their naval budget is greater than either those of the United States or of England. Useless to ask why they are building this fleet. Sooner or later the Empire will have to break away from Japan. If Canada endorses the cause of Australia, oui ships will anchor in the Pacific, on the Japanese side, bearing the brunt of the Japanese torpedo attacks. Will our rank of sister 
nation oblige us to subdue all the nations of the world?
Australia at the Imperial Conference of next June, will no doubt claim the support of the Empire and the sister nations. Whas attitude shall we take? That is the question. We must, notwithstanding our rank of sister nation, direct our policy as, being one of the countries of America, where our interests lie, and where we are to look for our support based upon those common interests (which are after all the most natural and the most lasting foundation. As far back as 1838, Lafontaine was of the same opinion and insisted on this point as of the most vital importance. He thus wrote to Mr. Ellice:
"It is not in your power to change our customs, our needs and specially our geographical position, although one of your newspapers has recently expressed such a desire. That is very British. It is absurd to think that we might have in view to become again a French possession. Such a motion would make the Canadians rise in a body. But you cannot prevent our being Americans, either that a sound policy on the part of England should prepare its northern colonies to independence, or that this lack of foresight should compel us to be gathered into the bosom of the Union. It is for you to avoid this, if you judge it convenient.
This is also the opinion of true soldiers, that it is absolutely absurd for Canada to think of a system of defence either by land or sea without first coming to an understanding with the United States. We should to-day more than ever take advantage of the Monroe doctrine, a British invention, on which Britain, the only European nation left on the American continent, all the others having been expelled, relies to safeguard, her interests in America (Canada and Newfoundland).
Through the intervention of Mr. Canning, a British statesman and Mr. Addington, British Ambassador at Washington, President Monroe decided to no more tolerate the conquest or the retaking of any part of the two Americas by any European power. We should direct our future policy in such a manner as to conclude a defensive alliance with the United States, the only nation that can and has an interest to give us an effective protection against Japan who might at any moment turn Canada into a new Belgium. But this alliance can only easily take place inasmuch as we will be independent, because the United States cannot undertake to protect us against all Great Britain's enemies. We should also think of forming an alliance with the republics to the south, Argentina, Brazil and Chile, so as to afford protection to the

whole American continent. It is ridiculous for Canada to try and build fleets and erect fortifications independently of our neighbours. It would be looked upon as a challenge, when they are addicted at present to a policy of armament without measure and they possess all the gold in the world. Since Mr. Lionel Curtis, states that there are but two possible alternatives to our future policy, either imperial partnership which would impose sacrifices and create burdens, or independence under the sovereignty of the King of England, we should choose this last alternative, the only one, owing to similarity of interests, of a nature to ensure our safety at the proper time. This was Lafontaine's opinion in 1838 as I explained a few moments ago, it was in 1852 Disraeli's opinion, in 1865, it was John Bright's opinion, also that of Lord Lisgar, Bishop Laroque and Bishop La Fliche, it was also that of Sir Charles Tupper and Sir John A Macdonald and also the opinion I believe of our late leader Sir Wilfrid Laurier.
Sir John A. Macdonald of whom the present Government party claim to be the successor spoke as follows:
When we become a nation of eight or nine millions of inhabitants our alliance will be worthy of being sought by the great nations of the earth.
And Sir Charles Tupper said:
We must ever retain the entire^ complete and independent management of our affairs.
Mr. Speaker, in closing my remarks, I believe that the most honourable, the most Canadian attitude that might adopt our delegates at the next Imperial conference, would be to cross the seas bearing in their heart the motto of the late leader of the Liberal party:	"Canada first, Canada
second, Canada forever."

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to make a speech, nor do I presume to conclude the debate. But I cannot let go unchallenged the suggestion thrown out by the hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Currie) that those who vote for the amendment of the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) will be taking an anti-British stand. I do not see how the hon. member can reconcile this view with what has just been said by the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) that the amendment is useless. The Prime Minister himself said in the conclusion of his address that he would not bind Parliament to any final decision; therefore the member for
Simcoe will admit that if he charges us with any anti-British feeling he must also conclude that the Prime Minister himself made an anti-British conclusion to his speech.
I do not intend, I repeat, to make a speech, and possibly I should crave the indulgence of the House for entering this debate after so many prominent members on both sides have taken part in it. But I wish to give the impressions, I would say, of a young member listening to the series of speeches that we have heard, and I should like to do so in a very untraditional way. First of all, I cannot see why on this occasion, as on several other occasions, the Government should charge the Opposition, when we move a resolution or an amendment to the motion for Supply, with bringing forward a motion of want of confidence. It seems to me that there is no logic in that conclusion, because we all know that a motion for Supply is very often made for the express purpose of permitting the discussion of a certain subject to take place. I do not wish to make any argument based upon the rules or traditions of the House; I repeat that I wish to give my own impression as a new member. But I do notice that the House is moved into Committee of Supply very often for the express purpose of permitting discussion, and to-day the motion was specially made on behalf of the Government, to allow the member for King's (Sir Robert Borden) and other members to make speeches about the coming conference in London. If we cannot move an amendment on such an occasion without being charged with expressing want of confidence in the Government, it means that when we have a discussion of this kind we cannot embody our attitude in an amendment and ask for the vote of the House on it without at the same time intimating that we wish to refuse Supply to the Government. Why, Mr. Speaker, in this particular case such a contention would be manifestly illogical because we are ready to vote Supply to defray the expenses of our Prime Minister in connection with his trip to London. We are not trying to prevent him from attending this conference; we are merely trying to have Parliament agree on the attitude he should take there.
The Prime Minister said that he could not go to the conference with a fixed programme because if he did so there would be no use for the conference. I cannot understand what that means. The Prime

Minister seems to feel that if he goes to London without a fixed programme, if he goes to voice his own opinion, then there is plenty of room for such a conference, but if instead of voicing his own opinion or even that of his own party he goes there with the opinion of the Parliament of Canada, there is, he would contend, no use for the conference. On the contrary, I think it is perfectly right to say that by moving this amendment we have shown our desire to strengthen hdg position rather than to weaken it in any way.
The Prime Minister has said that he will not arrive at any final decision which would be binding upon Parliament with regard to what we shall do in the future. But the Minister of Trade and Commerce says there is no use for this resolution; that Parliament might as well set forth the cut of the clothing, the shape of the suits that the Prime Minister should take to London. We are not concerned at all, Mr. Speaker, with the quality of the clothing that the Prime Minister will take to London. But we are concerned as to the quality of clothing that he will bring back from London to Canada. It is not so much, I will say, a question of clothing as it is a question of ties-the question of what ties the Prime Minister will bring back around his neck and wish to put around the necks of the Canadian people. I will go further and say that the Prime Minister-provided, of course, he accepts the resolution that we have been kind enough to move to-day-should not prolong his sojourn in London. Of course, it may be interesting for Lloyd George to know what the Prime Minister of Canada thinks of the Anglo-Japanese treaty, hut I humbly submit that we have Chinese puzzles at home which require the attention of the Prime Minister. If he would give some thought to Lord Shaughnessy's letter about the railway problem, or spend a couple of days urging the Minister of Marine to abandon his scheme of shipbuilding when ships are not needed, or give his attention to other home problems, it would be worth his while making his stay in London as short as required by the conference, and in any case not too long.
I must say that I was very much impressed by the speech made by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) to the effect that we are concerning ourselves altogether' too much in this House about foreign policies. Mr. Speaker, more foreign policy has been jammed into this half session than during the whole of our history. It seems that we cannont enter upon the 
consideration of any question, whether it be railways or canals or the debate on the Address or whatever it is, without getting an extra large supply of treatises on the League of Nations. I do not object to the" League of Nations; on the contrary I look very sympathetically upon this scheme. But I am afraid we are overfeeding the people with it, and the more we hear of it the less we are able to understand exactly what its aims are.
I repeat that by moving this resolution we were simply trying to strengthen the hand of the Prime Minister in London, in case, we will say, a resolution should be moved, not by a gang of robbers, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce insinuated so mildly, but by gentlemen on the other side or coming from other Dominions who might entertain opinions on certain matters different from those which we entertain in Canada. We were simply strengthening his position. We were allowing him to say not that we should avoid this and that we should avoid that, but that the Parliament of Canada is of opinion that we should not enter into such and such a bargain. That was our intention; if I understood the speeches delivered by hon. gentlemen on this side of the House, and I think it was a proper attitude to take. Instead of urging the leader of the Opposition to withdraw his motion, I am very sorry that such a wise parliamentarian and experienced politician as the Minister of Trade and Commerce did not urge the Prime Minister to accept that resolution and to go to London fortified by the feeling that the whole Parliament of Canada was behind him.
Mr. G., W. ANDREWS (Winnipeg Centre) : Mr. Speaker, I have looked forward with a good deal of pleasure to this debate, and I have not been disappointed. The speeches have been of a very high order, worthy of the great subject under discussion. I want to state very frankly my opinion on this subject, and I appreciate the opportunity to do so that has been afforded by the leader of the Government (Mr. Meighen). If my views do not coincide with the views of the people whom I represent, ample time remains for them to register their protest before the Prime Minister goes overseas.
In the first place, in my opinion, the great need in the world to-day, as regards the war and armaments, is disarmament, and disarmament, like charity, should begin at home. But having said that, I desire

also to point out that it is no use for one country to disarm to-day. We have long since passed that stage, and I must again point out to hon. members that not only Great Britain, but twenty-seven other countries took part in the last war as allies. The day of the little nation has gone, except in so far as it is supported by the opinion of civilization. Two things stand out in my mind. The first one is that if the leaders who declared war had
12 m. been called upon for one week [DOT]to undergo what our fighting men had to undergo in the salient at Ypres, the war would not have lasted very long. The second one, burned in with six-inch shells, is that if the countries of the world had spent half as much in peace propaganda as they spent in armaments, there would have been no war at all. Having said that-.and I have said it with a pur-t pose-I think the House will realize that, whatever else I may or may not be, I am not a jingo-imperialist.
I have listened to the amendment, and if it does not curtail the work of the Prime Minister, if it does not tie his hands, what good purpose does it serve? If it does tie his hands, Prime Minister Meighen becomes delegate Meighen, and that is a position which I would not accept myself, and I will not ask another man to do what I would not do myself. I would not ask the leader of the Opposition or the leader of the Government to do it.
I am not one of those men who believe in cast iron agreements. The British Empire has not been built in that way. There are a few men, as has already been pointed out to-day, here and everywhere, militarists, and mem who want everything bound up and fixed before they go on, who cannot work unless they have some precedents or authorities to go by. We find the same thing in every day business life. There are men who cannot work unless they get an order, and there are men who must have a precedent for everything, but such men never amount to much. As I have said, the British Empire has not been built in that way. We have always been fortunate enough to have men who could, in a commonsense way, deal with affairs as they came up, and if the time ever comes when the leaders of our nation require a precedent before they can act, or somebody else to give them an order, we can say goodbye to our greatness. But I would go a little further, and I would point out to hon. members that other countries are
just as anxious for peace as we are. . I venture the statement that Lloyd George wants peace just as much as I do. The British people have spent just as much blood and money and they are spending it now; the people of Australia, the people of South Africa have done the same thing. We are not going amongst enemies, we are going amongst friends, and this conference if it works at all, is going to work for peace.
Before resuming my seat, I think, for imperial reasons, it would be a mistake to let the Prime Minister go overseas from a divided House. It does not represent the spirit of Canada to send a representative overseas with only half the people or half the members of this House behind him. That has not a good effect, and it is effect -results-that we want. While any amendment that favours disarmament or peace always receives my sympathy, I think a mistake has been made in bringing this one forward to-day, and I ask the leader of the Opposition to withdraw it. If he can see his way to do that, he will never regret it.
